```
===== 428f0edc-Mathrix_AI_Coding_Challenge.docx
Coding Challenge: Live Armenian Transcription → English Translation

Oct 21, 2026 · @Sven Badalyan

Overview

Build a Python program that listens to a live conversation, transcribes spoken Armenian and prints an English translation in the terminal within 5 seconds, labelled by speaker.

Think of a video call: you speak into your microphone, the other participants come through your computer's audio output. The program captures both, works out who is speaking and shows what was said in Armenian and English, line by line, while the conversation is still running.

There is no single right architecture. We care as much about how you approach the problem as about the result.

Required features

1.  Two audio sources at once. Capture the microphone and the system audio output (the other side of a call) at the same time.

    -   On macOS this usually means a virtual loopback device such as BlackHole plus a Multi-Output Device, so the user still hears the call. On other systems, use the equivalent.

    -   Let the user pick the input devices, for example from a printed device list or by command-line flags.

2.  Armenian transcription. Turn spoken Armenian into Armenian text.

3.  English translation. Translate each transcribed segment into English.

4.  Speaker identification.

    -   Everything from the microphone is labelled Me.

    -   On the system-audio side, different people are told apart and labelled Speaker 1, Speaker 2 and so on. The same person should keep the same label for the whole session.

5.  Live terminal output. Each segment appears as it is processed, with time, speaker, Armenian original and English translation. For example:

[00:01:12] Speaker 1
HY: Բարև, ինչպե՞ս ես։
EN: Hi, how are you?
[00:01:15] Me
HY: Լավ եմ, շնորհակալություն։
EN: I'm fine, thank you.

The exact layout is up to you, as long as those four pieces of information are there.

Constraints

-   Latency: at most 5 seconds from the end of a spoken phrase to its English line in the terminal.

-   Local models only. Transcription, translation and speaker identification run on your own machine. No cloud speech or translation APIs.

-   Python. Any libraries and models you like, as long as they run locally.

-   Your hardware, your OS. It must run on the machine you bring to the interview. Apple Silicon is not required.

-   Choose your models deliberately. Armenian is a low-resource language, and model quality varies a lot. Explain in the README what you picked and why.

Out of scope

Keep it basic. You do not need:

-   a graphical interface (the terminal is enough)

-   an installer or packaged app

-   echo handling (when the speakers are picked up by the microphone)

-   recognising speakers by name, or remembering them across sessions

-   saving transcripts to a file

-   languages other than Armenian as input

If you finish early, spend the time making the core more reliable rather than adding features.

Deliverables

Send us a link to a Git repository containing:

1.  The source code.

2.  A README covering:

    -   how to set up and run it, including the audio device setup

    -   which models you chose, the alternatives you considered and why you decided as you did

    -   how the pieces fit together (a short architecture description is enough)

    -   known limitations and what you would improve with more time

3.  Your complete AI chat transcripts in a chats/ folder.

    -   We expect you to work with Claude Cowork for this project. Using any other AI assistant is not allowed. Export every conversation you had for this project, in full and unedited. This includes all other chat sessions you used in Claude Cowork, so export all sessions, not only the main one. That way all of your work can be tracked. Each session must be exported as its own Markdown (.md) file.

Do not commit model weights, audio recordings or API keys.

Timeline and the interview

You have one week from receiving this brief. We expect about 20 hours of work; please do not spend much more.

In the interview, which takes place on your own laptop:

1.  You start the program and we hold a short live conversation in Armenian with at least two people on the call side.

2.  We look at the output together and talk about what works, what does not and why.

3.  You walk us through your code and your decisions.

4.  You open your AI chat history in the tool you used. We look at the original conversations, not only the exported copies, so keep them available.

Make sure the program is installed and the audio setup works before the interview starts.

How we evaluate

We look at the result and, just as much, at how you got there.

  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Area                What we look at
  ------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Working method      How you broke the problem down, what you researched, and how you tested your assumptions. Seen in your chats and in the interview.

  Use of AI tools     Whether you steer the assistant or follow it. Clear prompts, checking its answers, and changing course when something does not work.

  Decisions           Model and architecture choices that are reasoned, with honest trade-offs.

  Live result         Does it run, is the Armenian recognised, is the English understandable, does it stay under 5 seconds, are speakers kept apart?

  Code                Readable structure and sensible separation of audio, transcription, translation and speaker parts.

  Communication       A README someone else can follow, and clear explanations in the interview.
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A solution that is honest about its limits beats one that hides them.
===== d70fccbb-Mathrix_AI_Vibe_Coding_Tips.docx
Vibe Coding: 10 Tips for Working with Claude Cowork

Mathrix AI · How we work: you are the architect, the AI is your team

1. Plan before you prompt

Start with a short PLAN.md: goal, modules, inputs/outputs of each module, risks, how you will test. Let Claude ask you clarifying questions first. A good plan saves more time than any prompt trick.

2. Build a walking skeleton first

Get the thinnest end-to-end version running (audio in → text → translation → terminal) before improving anything. Then always improve the weakest link, not the most fun one.

3. Isolate modules with clear inputs and outputs

When a codebase grows, take one module or workflow, define exactly what goes in and what comes out, and develop and test it in a separate chat. Merge it back into the main code only when it works on its own.

4. Write your tests and QA checks as you go

Collect test cases and critical QA questions during the work and write them down (e.g. TESTS.md or real test files). At the end you run against this list instead of checking the code from half-remembered ideas. Tests should come from the requirements, not from the code the AI just wrote.

5. Measure, don't guess

Build a small evaluation set early (e.g. a few short Armenian recordings with the correct text) and measure what matters: error rate, latency, speaker labels. Compare models with numbers, not impressions.

6. Give little, but the right context

Do not dump many files into a chat. Too much context makes the AI worse: it loses focus and starts to hallucinate. When a chat gets long, write a short handover (goal, current state, decisions, next step), start a new chat with it, and only go back to the old one to look something up.

7. Keep a decision log and project rules

Write important decisions with their reasons into DECISIONS.md, and stable rules (style, structure, "never do X") into a project instruction file. New chats then start with the same knowledge instead of re-deciding everything.

8. Read everything the AI writes, and keep it simple

Do not let the AI decide everything. It quickly adds irrelevant cases, silent fallbacks, timeouts and extra features to look "production-ready". Fallbacks hide where errors really are and make debugging slow. Prefer code that fails loudly and clearly.

9. Verify facts, models and libraries

The AI can invent APIs, parameters or model names, or describe models that do not exist for Armenian. Check the documentation, run the code yourself and ask the AI for its source when something sounds too good.

10. Commit small, step back early

Use Git, commit after every working step, and change one thing at a time. If the AI fails three times on the same problem, stop: go back to the last working commit, narrow the problem down to a small example, or rethink the approach instead of prompting the same thing again.

  In short: plan, split, measure, read, commit. Steer the AI instead of following it.
```

## 1. Requirements summary (from the brief only)

**The goal:** a Python terminal program that listens to a live call. It turns spoken Armenian into Armenian text, translates it, and prints the English **within 5 seconds**, with a label for who spoke.

### Mandatory features

| # | Requirement | What it means in practice |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Two audio sources at the same time** | Record your **microphone** and your **system audio output** (what you hear from the call) in parallel. The user must be able to **pick the devices**, from a printed list or with command-line flags. On Windows, the "equivalent" of BlackHole is WASAPI loopback (explained below). |
| 2 | **Armenian transcription** | Speech becomes Armenian text. |
| 3 | **English translation** | Each segment is translated into English. |
| 4 | **Speaker identification** | Everything from the mic is labelled **Me**. On the system-audio side, different people get **Speaker 1, Speaker 2…**, and each person **keeps the same label for the whole session**. |
| 5 | **Live terminal output** | Each segment shows **time, speaker, Armenian original and English translation**, printed as it is processed. You choose the layout. |

### Constraints
- **Latency ≤ 5 s**, measured from the *end of a spoken phrase* to its English line appearing.
- **Local models only.** Transcription, translation and speaker identification all run on your laptop. No cloud speech or translation APIs, paid or free.
- **Python**, with any local libraries or models.
- **Your hardware and OS.** It must run on the laptop you bring to the interview.
- **Choose models deliberately** and explain the choice in the README. They point out that Armenian is "low-resource", meaning there is little training data for it.

### Explicitly out of scope (we won't build these)
A GUI, an installer, echo handling, recognising speakers by name or across sessions, saving transcripts, and input languages other than Armenian. If there's spare time, it goes into **reliability, not features**.

### Deliverables (a Git repo link)
1. Source code.
2. A README covering: setup and run instructions, **including the audio device setup**; the models chosen, the alternatives considered and why; a short architecture description; known limitations and what you'd improve.
3. **A `chats/` folder** with **every** AI conversation for this project, **full and unedited**, **one Markdown file per session**. That includes side sessions, not just the main one. Only Claude Cowork is allowed: no other AI assistant.
4. **Never commit** model weights, audio recordings or API keys.

### The interview (this shapes what "done" means)
- A live Armenian conversation with **at least two people on the call side**, so the "Speaker 1 / Speaker 2" feature will really be tested.
- You walk them through the code and your decisions.
- They open your **original chat history in the app**, so **never delete any session**.
- The program and audio setup must already be installed and working before the interview starts.

### How they evaluate
Working method, how you steer the AI, your reasoning on decisions, the live result, code structure, and the README. Their key line: *"A solution that is honest about its limits beats one that hides them."*

---

## 2. Feasibility on your laptop

**Overall: feasible, but only with mid-sized models and careful choices.** The GPU memory (3 GB) and the 5-second limit are the real constraints, not the CPU.

| Resource | Verdict | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **GTX 1060, 3 GB VRAM** | ⚠️ Tight but workable | Enough for one speech-recognition model in "int8" form (weights compressed to 8-bit numbers, so they need about 4× less memory). Running the biggest Whisper model *and* a translation model on the GPU together probably won't fit. |
| **8 GB RAM** | ⚠️ Tight | The call app, a browser, Python and the models all share it. The translation model may need to run on the CPU and use RAM. We'll measure this. |
| **i5-8300H (4 cores)** | ✅ OK | Fine for audio capture, voice detection, the speaker model and possibly translation. Too slow for good speech recognition on its own. |
| **Windows 11** | ✅ Actually easier than macOS | Windows can record "what the speakers are playing" natively (**WASAPI loopback**). No BlackHole-style virtual driver is needed, and you still hear the call normally. |

### Biggest technical risks, ranked

1. **Armenian speech recognition quality.** This is the main risk. Whisper supports Armenian, but its error rate is much higher than for English, and smaller Whisper models are noticeably worse. Fine-tuned Armenian community models exist on Hugging Face, but quality varies, and some described online may be weak or misdescribed. **We'll only trust numbers we measure on your own recordings.**
2. **Speed vs. quality on a 3 GB Pascal GPU.** Two specific concerns, which I'll verify during setup rather than assume:
   - Your GPU's architecture (Pascal) is very slow at "float16" math, the usual GPU speed trick. We'll likely use **int8** instead.
   - I believe recent CUDA versions (CUDA 13) dropped Pascal support, so we may need to pin library versions built for **CUDA 12**.
3. **Speaker separation on the call side.** We need to tell two remote people apart *live*, from short segments of compressed call audio, without knowing beforehand how many people there are. This is the most experimental part. Short phrases ("Այո") carry little voice information, and people talking over each other will confuse it.
4. **The 5-second budget.** Rough budget: detecting that the phrase ended (~0.6 s) + transcription (~1–2.5 s) + translation (~0.3–0.8 s) + speaker embedding (~0.1 s). It fits, but **both streams share one GPU**. If you and a remote speaker talk at the same moment, one segment waits in a queue. Long monologues need a maximum segment length, or the "end of phrase" never comes.
5. **Whisper "hallucinations".** On silence or noise, Whisper sometimes invents text. Voice activity detection (VAD) reduces this a lot. VAD is a small model that decides "is someone talking right now?"
6. **Testing needs Armenian speakers.** To test speaker ID realistically you need recordings or calls with 2+ different voices. You'll need help from friends or family a few times.

---

## 3. Recommended technologies (to be confirmed by measurement)

| Part | Recommendation | Why | Limitations | Alternatives we'll compare |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Audio capture** | **`PyAudioWPatch`** or **`soundcard`**, both of which support WASAPI loopback | Records the mic and system output in parallel with no extra driver | Captures *all* system sounds, notifications included | VB-Audio Virtual Cable (a separate driver), or "Stereo Mix" if your sound card has it |
| **Voice detection / cutting into phrases** | **Silero VAD** | Small, fast, runs on CPU, widely used | Needs tuning: how much silence counts as "phrase ended" | WebRTC VAD (older, less accurate) |
| **Transcription (ASR)** | **`faster-whisper`**, a fast re-implementation of OpenAI Whisper that supports int8 | Speaks Armenian, about 4× faster than the original, fits 3 GB in int8 | Armenian accuracy is mediocre at small sizes; the large models may be too slow | Whisper small / medium / large-v3, Armenian fine-tuned Whisper checkpoints, Meta **MMS** (1,000+ languages including Armenian) |
| **Translation (MT)** | **Meta NLLB-200 distilled 600M**, run with CTranslate2 | Explicitly supports Armenian (`hye_Armn`), runs locally and fast in int8 | Short or broken sentences translate awkwardly; it translates the ASR's mistakes too | **Helsinki-NLP opus-mt-hy-en** (smaller and faster; I'll verify it exists and how good it is), Whisper's built-in "translate" mode |
| **Speaker identification** | **SpeechBrain ECAPA-TDNN** speaker embeddings + simple **online clustering** | An embedding turns a voice clip into a "fingerprint" vector. New segment → compare to known speakers → same person if similar enough, otherwise "Speaker N+1". Easy to explain, no account needed. | One threshold to tune; very short clips and overlapping speech fail | pyannote.audio (powerful but gated behind a Hugging Face token and heavier), Resemblyzer |
| **Plumbing** | Python 3.11, threads + queues, `argparse`, `pytest`, Git | Simple and readable; each module has clear inputs and outputs | Python threads are fine here because the heavy work happens in C++/CUDA | asyncio (more complex, no real gain) |

The architecture in one line:
`mic thread ─┐` / `loopback thread ─┤→ VAD → phrase queue → ASR → MT → (speaker ID for loopback only) → printer`

---

## 4. Development plan (~20 hours, 11 days until Nov 1)

That works out to roughly 2 hours a day, plus a buffer. The order follows tip #2: **get a working end-to-end skeleton first, then improve the weakest part.**

| # | Milestone | Hours | Done when… |
|---|---|---|---|
| **M0** | **Setup and planning docs**: Git repo, Python 3.11 venv, CUDA check, `PLAN.md`, `DECISIONS.md`, `TESTS.md`, a project rules file, `.gitignore` (weights, audio, keys) | 1.5 | `python -c` shows the GPU is visible to the libraries; docs committed |
| **M1** | **Audio capture**: list devices, choose them by flag, record mic + loopback *simultaneously* to test WAV files | 2 | You hear both recordings and they are clean, while a real call (e.g. Google Meet) is running |
| **M2** | **Walking skeleton**, mic only: VAD → small Whisper → NLLB → terminal print with timestamps | 2.5 | You speak Armenian and English lines appear, with latency printed |
| **M3** | **Evaluation set + ASR comparison**: ~15–20 short Armenian clips with correct text, a script that measures error rate (WER/CER) and speed per model | 3.5 | A small table of numbers decides the ASR model (recorded in DECISIONS.md) |
| **M4** | **Translation comparison**: 2–3 candidates on the same sentences, judged with your reading + speed | 1.5 | Translation model chosen with reasons |
| **M5** | **Both streams + speaker ID**: loopback stream joins; "Me" vs. Speaker 1/2/… clustering; tune the threshold on 2–3 voices | 3.5 | Two remote voices get stable separate labels in a test call |
| **M6** | **Latency and reliability**: measure end-of-phrase → print, cap segment length, filter hallucinations, handle the GPU queue | 2 | 95% of segments under 5 s in a 10-minute test call |
| **M7** | **README + rehearsal**: full interview simulation with 2+ people on the call side, from a fresh terminal | 2 | Someone could follow the README; dry run passes |
| | **Buffer** for surprises (CUDA issues, a model that disappoints) | 1.5 | |
| | **Total** | **20** | |

Each milestone ends with a commit. If something fails three times, we go back to the last working commit and narrow the problem down (tip #10).

## 5. How we'll test against the requirements

`TESTS.md` will be written from **the brief**, not from the code:

- **R1 Two sources:** both streams captured at once during a real call; the device list prints; the flags select devices; you can still hear the call.
- **R2 Transcription:** CER/WER (character and word error rate, i.e. the percentage of letters or words the model got wrong) on our eval clips, compared across models.
- **R3 Translation:** a fixed sentence list with reference English; you judge whether it's "understandable", as the brief puts it.
- **R4 Speakers:** mic is always "Me"; 2–3 remote voices get distinct labels that **stay stable for 10+ minutes**. We count wrong labels.
- **R5 Output:** each line has time, speaker, HY and EN.
- **Latency:** the program logs, for every segment, "phrase ended at X → printed at Y". We report the median, the worst case and the % under 5 s, with real numbers in the README.
- **Local only:** run with Wi-Fi off after models are downloaded. This is a strong, simple proof.
- **Repo hygiene:** a check that no `.wav`, model files or keys are tracked by Git.
- Small `pytest` unit tests for the logic parts: segmenting, clustering, formatting.

---

## 6. Preserving the AI chats in `chats/`

The brief requires **every** session to be exported **in full, unedited, as its own `.md` file**, and in the interview they'll look at the **originals in the app**. My proposal:

1. **Never delete or edit any session**, including failed experiments. Those count positively as "working method".
2. **One session per module** (tip #3 and #6), e.g. "Mathrix – main/planning", "Mathrix – audio capture", "Mathrix – ASR eval". Give them clear names so they're easy to find and export. When a chat gets long, I'll write a short **handover note** you paste into the next one.
3. **Keep a `chats/INDEX.md`** listing each session: date, topic, file name. That makes the export at the end easy to check for completeness.
4. **Export at the end** (and ideally once mid-way as a backup) using the app's own export, one file per session, without editing a single character. I don't know the exact export steps in your app version and won't guess. I can look it up in Anthropic's support docs if you'd like, and we should test exporting *this* session early so there are no surprises on Oct 31.
5. **This conversation is session #1** and must be included.
6. Don't use ChatGPT, Copilot or any other AI assistant, including the autocomplete in your code editor. Turn GitHub Copilot off in VS Code if it's on.

2. A README covering: setup and run instructions, **including the audio device setup**; the models chosen, the alternatives considered and why; a short architecture description; known limitations and what you'd improve.
3. **A `chats/` folder** with **every** AI conversation for this project, **full and unedited**, **one Markdown file per session**. That includes side sessions, not just the main one. Only Claude Cowork is allowed: no other AI assistant.
4. **Never commit** model weights, audio recordings or API keys.

### The interview (this shapes what "done" means)
- A live Armenian conversation with **at least two people on the call side**, so the "Speaker 1 / Speaker 2" feature will really be tested.
- You walk them through the code and your decisions.
- They open your **original chat history in the app**, so **never delete any session**.
- The program and audio setup must already be installed and working before the interview starts.

### How they evaluate
Working method, how you steer the AI, your reasoning on decisions, the live result, code structure, and the README. Their key line: *"A solution that is honest about its limits beats one that hides them."*

---

## 2. Feasibility on your laptop

**Overall: feasible, but only with mid-sized models and careful choices.** The GPU memory (3 GB) and the 5-second limit are the real constraints, not the CPU.

| Resource | Verdict | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **GTX 1060, 3 GB VRAM** | ⚠️ Tight but workable | Enough for one speech-recognition model in "int8" form (weights compressed to 8-bit numbers, so they need about 4× less memory). Running the biggest Whisper model *and* a translation model on the GPU together probably won't fit. |
| **8 GB RAM** | ⚠️ Tight | The call app, a browser, Python and the models all share it. The translation model may need to run on the CPU and use RAM. We'll measure this. |
| **i5-8300H (4 cores)** | ✅ OK | Fine for audio capture, voice detection, the speaker model and possibly translation. Too slow for good speech recognition on its own. |
| **Windows 11** | ✅ Actually easier than macOS | Windows can record "what the speakers are playing" natively (**WASAPI loopback**). No BlackHole-style virtual driver is needed, and you still hear the call normally. |

### Biggest technical risks, ranked

1. **Armenian speech recognition quality.** This is the main risk. Whisper supports Armenian, but its error rate is much higher than for English, and smaller Whisper models are noticeably worse. Fine-tuned Armenian community models exist on Hugging Face, but quality varies, and some described online may be weak or misdescribed. **We'll only trust numbers we measure on your own recordings.**
2. **Speed vs. quality on a 3 GB Pascal GPU.** Two specific concerns, which I'll verify during setup rather than assume:
   - Your GPU's architecture (Pascal) is very slow at "float16" math, the usual GPU speed trick. We'll likely use **int8** instead.
   - I believe recent CUDA versions (CUDA 13) dropped Pascal support, so we may need to pin library versions built for **CUDA 12**.
3. **Speaker separation on the call side.** We need to tell two remote people apart *live*, from short segments of compressed call audio, without knowing beforehand how many people there are. This is the most experimental part. Short phrases ("Այո") carry little voice information, and people talking over each other will confuse it.
4. **The 5-second budget.** Rough budget: detecting that the phrase ended (~0.6 s) + transcription (~1–2.5 s) + translation (~0.3–0.8 s) + speaker embedding (~0.1 s). It fits, but **both streams share one GPU**. If you and a remote speaker talk at the same moment, one segment waits in a queue. Long monologues need a maximum segment length, or the "end of phrase" never comes.
5. **Whisper "hallucinations".** On silence or noise, Whisper sometimes invents text. Voice activity detection (VAD) reduces this a lot. VAD is a small model that decides "is someone talking right now?"
6. **Testing needs Armenian speakers.** To test speaker ID realistically you need recordings or calls with 2+ different voices. You'll need help from friends or family a few times.

---

## 3. Recommended technologies (to be confirmed by measurement)

| Part | Recommendation | Why | Limitations | Alternatives we'll compare |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Audio capture** | **`PyAudioWPatch`** or **`soundcard`**, both of which support WASAPI loopback | Records the mic and system output in parallel with no extra driver | Captures *all* system sounds, notifications included | VB-Audio Virtual Cable (a separate driver), or "Stereo Mix" if your sound card has it |
| **Voice detection / cutting into phrases** | **Silero VAD** | Small, fast, runs on CPU, widely used | Needs tuning: how much silence counts as "phrase ended" | WebRTC VAD (older, less accurate) |
| **Transcription (ASR)** | **`faster-whisper`**, a fast re-implementation of OpenAI Whisper that supports int8 | Speaks Armenian, about 4× faster than the original, fits 3 GB in int8 | Armenian accuracy is mediocre at small sizes; the large models may be too slow | Whisper small / medium / large-v3, Armenian fine-tuned Whisper checkpoints, Meta **MMS** (1,000+ languages including Armenian) |
| **Translation (MT)** | **Meta NLLB-200 distilled 600M**, run with CTranslate2 | Explicitly supports Armenian (`hye_Armn`), runs locally and fast in int8 | Short or broken sentences translate awkwardly; it translates the ASR's mistakes too | **Helsinki-NLP opus-mt-hy-en** (smaller and faster; I'll verify it exists and how good it is), Whisper's built-in "translate" mode |
| **Speaker identification** | **SpeechBrain ECAPA-TDNN** speaker embeddings + simple **online clustering** | An embedding turns a voice clip into a "fingerprint" vector. New segment → compare to known speakers → same person if similar enough, otherwise "Speaker N+1". Easy to explain, no account needed. | One threshold to tune; very short clips and overlapping speech fail | pyannote.audio (powerful but gated behind a Hugging Face token and heavier), Resemblyzer |
| **Plumbing** | Python 3.11, threads + queues, `argparse`, `pytest`, Git | Simple and readable; each module has clear inputs and outputs | Python threads are fine here because the heavy work happens in C++/CUDA | asyncio (more complex, no real gain) |

The architecture in one line:
`mic thread ─┐` / `loopback thread ─┤→ VAD → phrase queue → ASR → MT → (speaker ID for loopback only) → printer`

---

That works out to roughly 2 hours a day, plus a buffer. The order follows tip #2: **get a working end-to-end skeleton first, then improve the weakest part.**

| # | Milestone | Hours | Done when… |

| **M0** | **Setup and planning docs**: Git repo, Python 3.11 venv, CUDA check, `PLAN.md`, `DECISIONS.md`, `TESTS.md`, a project rules file, `.gitignore` (weights, audio, keys) | 1.5 | `python -c` shows the GPU is visible to the libraries; docs committed |
| **M1** | **Audio capture**: list devices, choose them by flag, record mic + loopback *simultaneously* to test WAV files | 2 | You hear both recordings and they are clean, while a real call (e.g. Google Meet) is running |

| **M4** | **Translation comparison**: 2–3 candidates on the same sentences, judged with your reading + speed | 1.5 | Translation model chosen with reasons |
| **M5** | **Both streams + speaker ID**: loopback stream joins; "Me" vs. Speaker 1/2/… clustering; tune the threshold on 2–3 voices | 3.5 | Two remote voices get stable separate labels in a test call |
| **M6** | **Latency and reliability**: measure end-of-phrase → print, cap segment length, filter hallucinations, handle the GPU queue | 2 | 95% of segments under 5 s in a 10-minute test call |
| **M7** | **README + rehearsal**: full interview simulation with 2+ people on the call side, from a fresh terminal | 2 | Someone could follow the README; dry run passes |
| | **Buffer** for surprises (CUDA issues, a model that disappoints) | 1.5 | |
| | **Total** | **20** | |

Each milestone ends with a commit. If something fails three times, we go back to the last working commit and narrow the problem down (tip #10).

## 5. How we'll test against the requirements

`TESTS.md` will be written from **the brief**, not from the code:

- **R1 Two sources:** both streams captured at once during a real call; the device list prints; the flags select devices; you can still hear the call.
- **R2 Transcription:** CER/WER (character and word error rate, i.e. the percentage of letters or words the model got wrong) on our eval clips, compared across models.
- **R3 Translation:** a fixed sentence list with reference English; you judge whether it's "understandable", as the brief puts it.
- **R4 Speakers:** mic is always "Me"; 2–3 remote voices get distinct labels that **stay stable for 10+ minutes**. We count wrong labels.
- **R5 Output:** each line has time, speaker, HY and EN.
- **Latency:** the program logs, for every segment, "phrase ended at X → printed at Y". We report the median, the worst case and the % under 5 s, with real numbers in the README.
- **Local only:** run with Wi-Fi off after models are downloaded. This is a strong, simple proof.
- **Repo hygiene:** a check that no `.wav`, model files or keys are tracked by Git.
- Small `pytest` unit tests for the logic parts: segmenting, clustering, formatting.

---

```
**Short answer:** PyTorch 2.14 is the last release with a prebuilt Pascal wheel, and the CUDA 12.6 (cu126) variant is the only one that covered Pascal.

- **Wheel variants:** The article says CUDA 12.8 and 12.9 builds already dropped Maxwell and Pascal support, and CUDA 13.x doesn't support architectures below Turing (sm_75). It states that "CUDA 12.6 was the only remaining build covering them."
- **Last version:** PyTorch 2.14 (`cu126` index) is the last release with a prebuilt Pascal wheel.
- **Dates:**
  - CUDA 12.6 builds are removed from nightly on Monday, 7 September 2026.
  - PyTorch 2.15 drops CUDA 12.6 binaries entirely. The article doesn't give a 2.15 release date.
  - The 2.14 final RC was available August 27, 2026. The article doesn't state the 2.14 release date.
- **After 2.15:** Pascal users must stay on 2.14 or earlier, or build from source with a CUDA 12.x toolkit.

The article's table lists Pascal only as sm_60 and doesn't mention sm_61 specifically, so I'm treating sm_61 as falling under Pascal.
```

## What I verified, and why it matters

**Your GPU is from NVIDIA's "Pascal" generation, which the ML world is phasing out.** I checked:

- PyTorch (the main ML library) says on its official forum that its **CUDA 12.8+ builds already dropped Pascal**, **CUDA 13 doesn't support it at all**, and **PyTorch 2.14 with the `cu126` build is the last version with ready-made Pascal support**.
- NVIDIA confirmed that the **580 driver branch is the last to support Pascal**. Your 582.28 is from that branch. **Don't install a newer GPU driver before the interview.** Your current driver is the one that's supported.

**What this means for us (a small design change):** I'll keep **PyTorch on the CPU only** and run the heavy models through **CTranslate2**, the engine behind `faster-whisper` and also used for NLLB. CTranslate2 ships its own GPU libraries, so it doesn't depend on PyTorch's Pascal support. The small models (voice detection, speaker fingerprints) are fast enough on the CPU anyway. That sidesteps the problem instead of fighting it.

**Still unverified:** whether current CTranslate2 builds include kernels for your exact GPU (compute capability 6.1), and how fast int8 is on it. My search didn't give a clear answer, so the **first real test will be a GPU smoke test**. If it fails, we pin an older CTranslate2 version, and we'll know on day 1 instead of day 8.

**Disk:** model downloads go to `C:\Users\User\.cache` by default and can take 5–10 GB. I'll configure the virtual environment and model cache to live on **D:** inside `D:\Em\mathrix`, but excluded from Git.

```
**Per-capability behavior for these types** (from the GPU fallback table):

| Compute capability | int8 variants | float16 | bfloat16 |
|---|---|---|---|

**What happens when a type isn't supported:** Yes, there is a fallback. The runtime uses the saved type when the platform supports it. Otherwise, "the library converts the model weights to another optimized type." The table above gives the fallback type for each case.
```

The venv works: Python 3.12.1, with pip running from `D:\Em\mathrix\.venv`. You can run `git status` whenever convenient; it should report a clean working tree.

Before proposing the GPU test, I checked the official documentation. Here's what it says, and how it affects us.

## What the documentation says

**1. Your GPU supports the fast mode we planned.** The CTranslate2 quantization guide says `int8` works on "Compute Capability ≥ 7.0 **or Compute Capability 6.1**". Compute capability 6.1 is exactly your GTX 1060. ✅

**2. It hides a "silent fallback".** The same page says that if you ask your GPU for `float16`, the library quietly **switches to `float32`** without telling you. That's slower and uses twice the memory. This is exactly the kind of silent fallback our `CLAUDE.md` rules warn about. So we'll always request **`int8_float32`** explicitly. That's the type your GPU actually runs, and the test will print which types the library reports as supported.

**3. On Windows, the GPU needs two extra NVIDIA libraries.** These are **cuBLAS for CUDA 12** and **cuDNN 9**. The faster-whisper README offers two ways to get them:

| Option | How | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A (my recommendation)** | Install NVIDIA's official pip packages `nvidia-cublas-cu12` and `nvidia-cudnn-cu12` **into the venv** | Everything stays inside `.venv`, easy to reproduce from the README, no system changes | The README calls this method "Linux only". Windows wheels exist (I confirmed cuDNN has a `win_amd64` build on PyPI), but our script must tell Windows where the DLLs are |
| B | Third-party archive ("Purfview's whisper-standalone-win"), extracted and added to PATH | The README's suggested route for Windows | Third-party copies of NVIDIA files, manual PATH change, harder to document |
| C | Official NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit + cuDNN installers | The "proper" system install | Several GB on your nearly full C: drive; a system-wide change |

I recommend **A**, with **C** as the fallback if A fails. The test's job is to find out whether option A really works on Windows, rather than us trusting it.

## Proposed next step (two parts, both need your OK)

**Part 1: you run the installs (about 1–1.5 GB download).**

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --upgrade pip
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --no-cache-dir faster-whisper nvidia-cublas-cu12 nvidia-cudnn-cu12
```

What each line does:

- The first line updates pip inside the venv. Your 23.2.1 is from 2023, and old pip sometimes picks the wrong package versions.
- The second line installs the three packages into `.venv` only.
- `--no-cache-dir` stops pip from storing another copy of these large downloads on your C: drive.

**Part 2: I write `scripts/gpu_smoke_test.py`, and you run it.** It will:

1. Point Windows at the NVIDIA DLL folders inside the venv.
2. Print the number of GPUs CTranslate2 sees, and **which compute types it supports** (we expect `int8_float32` in the list).
3. Download Whisper **tiny** (about 75 MB) into `D:\Em\mathrix\models\`. That folder is already excluded by `.gitignore`.
4. Run it on the GPU with `int8_float32` on 5 seconds of generated test audio, and print the time taken. The text output itself doesn't matter. This step proves that the speech model's GPU parts (which need cuDNN) really run.
5. **Fail with a clear error message** if any step doesn't work, with no fallback to the CPU.

If it passes, ENV-4 in `TESTS.md` gets ticked, and D-002 in `DECISIONS.md` moves from "pending" to "verified". Then we can start M1 (audio capture).

**Do you approve Part 1 (the installs) and Part 2 (me writing the test script)?** You can approve just Part 1 first if you prefer to go one at a time.

- [faster-whisper README (GPU requirements)](https://github.com/SYSTRAN/faster-whisper)
- [CTranslate2 Quantization guide (int8 on compute capability 6.1; fallback table)](https://opennmt.net/CTranslate2/quantization.html)
- [CTranslate2 Installation guide](https://opennmt.net/CTranslate2/installation.html)
- [nvidia-cudnn-cu12 on PyPI (Windows wheel available)](https://pypi.org/project/nvidia-cudnn-cu12/#files)

I've created `scripts/gpu_smoke_test.py`, about 90 lines, and checked that the Python syntax is valid. It's the only file changed, and you can open it in VS Code to read along with this explanation.

## What the script does, part by part

**Settings at the top**
- `MODELS_DIR` is `D:\Em\mathrix\models`, where the model gets downloaded. Git ignores it.
- `COMPUTE_TYPE = "int8_float32"` is the explicit choice we discussed, so the library has nothing to silently switch.
- `SAMPLE_RATE = 16000`, because Whisper expects audio at 16,000 samples per second.

**`add_nvidia_dlls_to_search_path()`**

This finds the `bin` folders inside `.venv\Lib\site-packages\nvidia\` that hold the cuBLAS and cuDNN DLLs. It then tells Windows about them in two ways:
- `os.add_dll_directory` covers DLLs that Python loads itself.
- Adding them to `PATH` covers DLLs that CTranslate2 loads later, when the speech model first runs.

It has to run *before* `import ctranslate2`, which is why that import sits inside `main()` rather than at the top. If no NVIDIA folders are found, it stops with an error.

**`main()`, in 4 printed steps:**
1. Register the DLL folders and print each one.
2. Print the CTranslate2 version, the number of GPUs it sees (it **stops if 0**), and the supported compute types (it **stops if `int8_float32` is missing**).
3. Load Whisper **tiny** on `cuda` and print the load time.
4. Generate 5 seconds of a quiet 440 Hz tone and transcribe it **twice** with `language="hy"`, printing the time for each run. The first run includes one-time warm-up, so the second time is the realistic one. **The text output doesn't matter.** Whisper may print nothing, or nonsense, for a tone. What matters is that the GPU parts ran without crashing.

There's **no `try/except` and no CPU fallback** anywhere. If something breaks, you'll see Python's full error message, which is what we want.

## Run it

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\gpu_smoke_test.py
```

**Expected:** the 4 steps, ending with `SUCCESS: Whisper runs on the GPU with int8_float32`.

**Things you may see that are fine:**
- Download progress bars on the first run.
- A **warning about "symlinks"** from Hugging Face. On Windows without Developer Mode, it stores files as copies instead of shortcuts. That's harmless.

**If it fails**, paste the **complete output**. Different errors point to different causes:
- A message mentioning `cudnn...dll` or `cublas...dll` "not found" or "could not load" means Windows can't find the DLLs.
- A message like "no kernel image is available" means the libraries don't support your GPU generation. The likely fix then is an older cuDNN or cuBLAS version.

I've created `scripts/gpu_smoke_test.py`, about 90 lines, and checked that the Python syntax is valid. It's the only file changed, and you can open it in VS Code to read along with this explanation.

## What the script does, part by part

**Settings at the top**
- `MODELS_DIR` is `D:\Em\mathrix\models`, where the model gets downloaded. Git ignores it.
- `COMPUTE_TYPE = "int8_float32"` is the explicit choice we discussed, so the library has nothing to silently switch.
- `SAMPLE_RATE = 16000`, because Whisper expects audio at 16,000 samples per second.

**`add_nvidia_dlls_to_search_path()`**

This finds the `bin` folders inside `.venv\Lib\site-packages\nvidia\` that hold the cuBLAS and cuDNN DLLs. It then tells Windows about them in two ways:
- `os.add_dll_directory` covers DLLs that Python loads itself.
- Adding them to `PATH` covers DLLs that CTranslate2 loads later, when the speech model first runs.

It has to run *before* `import ctranslate2`, which is why that import sits inside `main()` rather than at the top. If no NVIDIA folders are found, it stops with an error.

**`main()`, in 4 printed steps:**
1. Register the DLL folders and print each one.
2. Print the CTranslate2 version, the number of GPUs it sees (it **stops if 0**), and the supported compute types (it **stops if `int8_float32` is missing**).
3. Load Whisper **tiny** on `cuda` and print the load time.
4. Generate 5 seconds of a quiet 440 Hz tone and transcribe it **twice** with `language="hy"`, printing the time for each run. The first run includes one-time warm-up, so the second time is the realistic one. **The text output doesn't matter.** Whisper may print nothing, or nonsense, for a tone. What matters is that the GPU parts ran without crashing.

There's **no `try/except` and no CPU fallback** anywhere. If something breaks, you'll see Python's full error message, which is what we want.

Hypothesis confirmed. Run 2 dropped from **4.01 s to 0.67 s** with no other change. The output text also shows *why* the earlier run was slow.

## What happened

**The "A-A-A-A…" text is a classic Whisper hallucination.** Given a tone with no speech, the model got stuck repeating the same token until it hit its maximum output length.

- **Before:** Whisper noticed that its output was suspiciously repetitive. Internally it measures a "compression ratio": very repetitive text compresses extremely well, which is a sign of garbage. So it **retried several times** and finally threw the text away. Result: empty text, but 4 s spent.
- **Now:** with `temperature=0.0` it decoded once and **kept the garbage**. Result: fast, but wrong.

Even 0.67 s is a pessimistic number. Whisper produced about 200 "A-" pieces of text here, while 5 seconds of real speech usually produces far fewer, so real speech should be faster still.

## What this teaches us for the real program

1. **Retries multiply latency.** With a 5-second budget, we can't let Whisper silently decode the same phrase 6 times. We'll control this setting deliberately.
2. **Without retries, garbage gets through.** So **non-speech must never reach Whisper**: that's the job of voice activity detection (Silero VAD), which we already planned. We may also need a visible check for repetitive output. We'll decide that in M2/M3 based on real speech, not now.
3. **The first transcription is slower** (0.91 s vs 0.67 s, a one-time GPU warm-up). The real program should do one warm-up run at start-up, so your first sentence in the interview isn't the slow one.
4. **What this does *not* tell us:** the speed of the *larger* models we'll actually need for Armenian (small, medium, large-v3), or their accuracy. That's M3, measured on your real recordings.

## M1: audio capture

**Goal (brief requirement 1):** capture the **microphone and the system audio at the same time**, and let the user **choose the devices** from a printed list or with command-line flags. M1 only records and saves test files. Transcription comes in M2.

### A few audio concepts, in simple terms

- **Sample rate:** how many times per second the sound is measured. Your Realtek devices probably run at **48,000 Hz**, but Whisper expects **16,000 Hz**. So we'll **resample** (convert), and we'll do it in our code, explicitly.
- **Channels:** the loopback of your speakers is **stereo** (left + right). Speech models want **mono**, so we average the two channels.
- **Chunks and threads:** audio arrives in small blocks (for example 20–30 ms each). Each device gets its own reader, running in parallel (a thread), and puts its blocks into a **queue**: a waiting line that the rest of the program takes from. Two devices means two readers, and that's how we capture "at the same time".
- **Timestamps:** each block is stamped with the time it arrived. Later, this gives us the `[00:01:12]` time and lets us measure the 5-second latency.

### Library choice (checked just now on PyPI)

| | **PyAudioWPatch** (recommended) | soundcard |
|---|---|---|
| Last release | **0.2.12.9, Oct 6, 2026**, actively maintained | 0.4.6; last changelog entry Jan 2026 |
| Python 3.12 Windows build | ✅ Yes | Pure Python, so yes |
| How loopback works | Loopback devices appear as **extra input devices** in the device list, so the mic and the system audio use **the same code** | Separate loopback API |
| Known issues | One thing to test (below) | Its own page lists Windows problems: garbage audio when recording a single channel, block size sometimes ignored, buffer underruns |

**One behaviour to verify, not assume:** I've read that WASAPI loopback may deliver *no data at all* while nothing is playing, rather than delivering silence. PyAudioWPatch's page doesn't say either way. It matters for our timestamps, so the M1 test will check it explicitly.

### M1 sub-steps (one at a time, each with your approval)

1. **Install `PyAudioWPatch`**: one small package, into the venv.
2. **`scripts/list_devices.py`** prints every device with its number, name, sample rate, channels and whether it's a loopback device. You run it and we pick your mic and the "Динамики [Loopback]" device. (R1-1)
3. **The capture module** (`audio_capture.py`), plus **`scripts/record_test.py --mic N --system N --seconds 15`**. It records both devices at the same time into two WAV files in `recordings/`, which Git ignores. (R1-2, R1-3)
4. **Real test:** play an Armenian YouTube video (or a Meet call) while speaking into the mic, with headphones on. Then listen to both files: is the mic file only you, and the system file only the video? Do you still hear the audio normally while recording? (R1-4) We'll also record a few seconds of silence to check the behaviour above.
5. Tick the tests, record the library decision in `DECISIONS.md`, and commit.

### A suggestion about chat sessions

This chat is getting long, and the Mathrix tips (#3, #6) recommend developing each module in its own session, starting from a short **handover note** (goal, current state, decisions, next step). If you agree:
- I'd write `HANDOVER.md` now (one new file).
- You'd start a new session named, say, "Mathrix 02 – audio capture", and add it to `chats/INDEX.md`.
- This session stays untouched for export and for the interview.

```
# Project rules (read at the start of every chat)

## Source of truth
- The official Mathrix AI challenge brief defines the requirements. Do not invent requirements.
- Out of scope (do not build): GUI, installer, echo handling, naming/remembering speakers across sessions, saving transcripts, non-Armenian input.
- Spare time goes into reliability of the core, not new features.

## Hard constraints
- Transcription, translation and speaker identification run locally. No cloud speech/translation APIs, no paid APIs.
- Never commit model weights, audio recordings, API keys or secrets.
- Never paste passwords, tokens or other people's personal data into any chat — chats are submitted unedited.
- Only Claude Cowork is used as AI assistant for this project.

## Environment
- Windows 11, GTX 1060 3 GB (Pascal), 8 GB RAM, Python 3.12 via `py -3.12`, venv at `D:\Em\mathrix\.venv`.
- Do not update the NVIDIA driver (see DECISIONS.md D-005).
- The user runs all commands in a normal (non-admin) PowerShell from `D:\Em\mathrix` and pastes the output back.

## Code style
- Keep audio, segmentation, ASR, translation, speakers and output in separate modules with clear inputs/outputs (see PLAN.md).
- Keep it simple and readable. Fail loudly with clear errors; no silent fallbacks, no hidden retries or timeouts.
- Do not add features or edge-case handling that the brief does not ask for.

## Way of working
- Ask before installing software, deleting files or making major changes.
- One change at a time; commit after every working step.
- Verify model names, APIs and parameters in official docs before using them; cite the source.
- Decide models by measurement (TESTS.md, eval set), not impressions.
- Record important decisions with reasons in DECISIONS.md.
- If something fails three times, stop, go back to the last working commit and narrow the problem down.
- Explain technical concepts in simple English.
```

## M1, sub-step 1: install PyAudioWPatch

**What it is:** a version of the well-known PyAudio library (Python's interface to PortAudio, a cross-platform audio library) with **WASAPI loopback support added**. Your speakers' "what's playing" signal then appears as one more input device, so the mic and the system audio are recorded with the same code.

**Commands** (from `D:\Em\mathrix`, normal PowerShell):

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install PyAudioWPatch==0.2.12.9
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -c "import pyaudiowpatch as pyaudio; print(pyaudio.get_portaudio_version_text())"
```

What each one does:

- The **first** installs the exact version we checked on PyPI (0.2.12.9, Oct 6, 2026). Pinning the version means we install what we researched, not whatever is newest today.
- The **second** checks that Python can load it, by printing the version of PortAudio, the C library underneath. It doesn't open any audio device yet.

**Expected:** `Successfully installed PyAudioWPatch-0.2.12.9`, and then a line like `PortAudio V19.7.0-devel...`. The exact text doesn't matter, as long as there's no error.

```python
"""List WASAPI audio devices (milestone M1, TESTS.md R1-1).

Shows only WASAPI devices: loopback (recording what the speakers play) exists
only in WASAPI, so we use WASAPI for the microphone too.

Run from the project folder:
    .\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe scripts\\list_devices.py
"""

import pyaudiowpatch as pyaudio


def device_type(info: dict) -> str:
    if info["isLoopbackDevice"]:          # field added by PyAudioWPatch
        return "LOOPBACK"
    if info["maxInputChannels"] > 0:
        return "INPUT"
    return "OUTPUT"


def main() -> None:
    p = pyaudio.PyAudio()
    try:
        wasapi = p.get_host_api_info_by_type(pyaudio.paWASAPI)
        default_mic = wasapi["defaultInputDevice"]
        default_loopback = p.get_default_wasapi_loopback()["index"]

        print(f"WASAPI devices (host API index {wasapi['index']}):\n")
        print(f"{'idx':>4}  {'type':<8}  {'ch':>2}  {'rate':>6}  name")
        for i in range(p.get_device_count()):
            info = p.get_device_info_by_index(i)
            if info["hostApi"] != wasapi["index"]:
                continue
            kind = device_type(info)
            channels = info["maxInputChannels"] if kind != "OUTPUT" else info["maxOutputChannels"]
            marker = ""
            if i == default_mic:
                marker = "   <-- default microphone"
            elif i == default_loopback:
                marker = "   <-- loopback of default speakers"
            print(f"{i:>4}  {kind:<8}  {channels:>2}  {int(info['defaultSampleRate']):>6}  {info['name']}{marker}")

        print("\nUse an INPUT index for --mic and a LOOPBACK index for --system.")
    finally:
        p.terminate()  # release PortAudio even if something above fails
```

## How it works

- **`device_type()`** decides the label. A loopback device is checked **first**, because loopback devices also report input channels: they're recordable, like a mic. Without that order, they'd be mislabelled as `INPUT`.
- **`p = pyaudio.PyAudio()`** starts PortAudio, the audio library underneath.
- **`get_host_api_info_by_type(paWASAPI)`** finds WASAPI and Windows' default mic number.
- **`get_default_wasapi_loopback()`** finds the loopback copy of your default speakers.
- **The loop** goes over all devices, **skips any that aren't WASAPI**, and prints one line per device with its markers.
- **`try / finally: p.terminate()`** always releases the audio system cleanly, even if an error happens. This **doesn't hide errors**: they still show in full. It only makes sure the clean-up runs.
- **No error handling beyond that.** If a field name like `isLoopbackDevice` were wrong, you'd see a `KeyError` naming it.

## Sub-step 3: capture both devices at the same time (design, before I write anything)

### Files

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `hylive/audio_capture.py` | The reusable **capture module**: the first real piece of the program. "hylive" stands for Armenian + live; it's just a package name, and you can suggest another. |
| `hylive/__init__.py` | An empty file that makes `hylive` a Python package |
| `scripts/record_test.py` | A test tool that uses the module to record both devices into two WAV files |

### How capture works (simple version)

- **Callback mode.** For each device we open a PortAudio "stream" and give it a small function, the *callback*. PortAudio calls it **on its own background thread** every time a new block of audio arrives, roughly every 10–20 ms. So two devices automatically means two parallel readers. We don't have to manage threads ourselves.
- The callback does almost nothing: it stamps the block with the current time and puts it in a **queue**. Callbacks must be quick, or audio gets lost, so all heavy work happens elsewhere.
- **The module's output:** `AudioChunk(source="mic" or "system", data, captured_at)`. That matches the interface written in `PLAN.md`.
- **Format for now:** the devices' **native format** (48 kHz, 2 channels, 16-bit). The **conversion to 16 kHz mono is deliberately postponed to M2**. There are a few ways to do it, with different quality/dependency trade-offs, and I'd rather decide that as its own step. For M1 we only want to prove that the capture is correct, and native-format WAVs are the honest way to listen to that.

### What `record_test.py` does

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\record_test.py --mic 9 --system 10 --seconds 15
```

1. Prints which devices it opened, by number and name.
2. Records both devices **at the same time** for 15 seconds.
3. Saves `recordings/<time>_mic.wav` and `recordings/<time>_system.wav`. The `recordings/` folder is ignored by Git.
4. **Prints diagnostics per stream:**
   - **Seconds of audio received vs. seconds of wall-clock time.** This directly answers our open question. If the system stream received, say, 4 s of audio during a 15 s recording while nothing was playing, then loopback really skips silence, and we must handle that in M2.
   - **Peak level**, so we know at a glance whether the file is silent.
   - **Count of "overflow" warnings** from PortAudio, meaning audio was lost because a reader was too slow. Shown, never hidden.

### One design question for you

If `--mic` / `--system` aren't given, should the program:
- **(a)** use **Windows' default mic and the default speakers' loopback**, and **print clearly which ones it chose**? This is convenient, and since the choice is printed it's not a hidden fallback. Or
- **(b)** refuse to start and ask for the flags? That's stricter, but more typing every time.

I recommend **(a)**. The brief requires that the user *can* pick the devices, not that they *must*.

### Not in this step

No resampling, no voice detection, no transcription. One thing at a time.

## `hylive/audio_capture.py`: the reusable module

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AudioChunk:
    source: str          # "mic" or "system"
    data: bytes          # raw 16-bit samples, channels interleaved
    captured_at: float   # time.monotonic() when the block arrived
```

This is **what the module outputs**, the interface from `PLAN.md`. `time.monotonic()` is a clock that never jumps, even if Windows adjusts the time, so it's the right clock for measuring latency later.

```python
    def _callback(self, in_data, frame_count, time_info, status):
        if status:
            self.status_flag_count += 1
        self.out_queue.put(AudioChunk(self.source, in_data, time.monotonic()))
        return (None, pyaudio.paContinue)
```

This is **the heart of the module**. PortAudio calls it on its own background thread every 10 ms per device (`FRAMES_PER_BUFFER = 480` at 48 kHz). It stamps the block, puts it in the queue and returns immediately. If PortAudio reports a problem (`status`), it's **counted and later shown**, never ignored.

Other parts:
- **`get_device()`** checks that a device number is a WASAPI device that can be recorded. If not, it raises an error that tells you to run `list_devices.py`.
- **`default_mic()` / `default_loopback()`** implement your option **(a)**.
- **`DeviceCapture.start()` / `stop()`** open and close one device's stream, using its native rate and channels.

## `scripts/record_test.py`: the test tool

1. It reads `--mic`, `--system` and `--seconds`. Without the device flags it uses the Windows defaults and **prints that it did**.
2. It **refuses mixed-up devices**: a loopback passed as `--mic`, or a normal mic passed as `--system`, gives a clear error.
3. It starts both captures, waits, stops both, and sorts the received blocks by source.
4. For each stream it writes a WAV file to `recordings/` and prints:
   - **audio received** vs. **wall-clock time**: this answers the "does loopback skip silence?" question;
   - **first block delay** and **largest gap between blocks**: a big gap would mean that audio stopped arriving at some point;
   - **peak level**, from 0 to 1, showing whether there was sound at all;
   - **problem flags**: how many blocks PortAudio reported trouble with.

## Results

**System stream: 0 blocks in 15 seconds.** This settles the open question from the handover. **WASAPI loopback delivers no data at all while nothing is playing.** It doesn't send silence; it sends nothing.

This matters for M2. Imagine a remote speaker finishes a sentence and the call goes completely quiet. The voice detector waits for "silence after speech" to decide the phrase has ended, but no audio arrives, so the phrase might never be closed and printed. Two possible solutions, to decide in M2:
- The program itself plays an inaudible silent stream on the speakers, which keeps loopback delivering data continuously. This is a commonly mentioned workaround, but I'll verify it actually works here rather than assume.
- The segmenter also closes a phrase when no new audio arrives for a while, based on the clock.

Whether call apps like Meet keep the audio stream "open" even when nobody talks is also unknown. We'll test that later. I'll record this as finding **D-010**.

**Mic stream: capture works, but the level is suspiciously low.**
- ✅ 15.0 s received in 1501 blocks of 10 ms, no gaps (largest 16 ms), 0 problem flags. The capture itself is correct.
- ⚠️ **Peak level 0.003.** That's very quiet. Normal speech close to a laptop mic usually peaks somewhere around 0.05–0.5. At 0.003, the file is almost silent.

Yes. Let's narrow it down before changing anything. My leading suspect is **the headphones themselves**, not the code.

## Why I suspect the headphones

Most laptops like yours have **one combined headphone/microphone jack**. When something is plugged in, the Realtek driver often **switches the "Микрофон" input from the laptop's built-in mic to the jack**, while keeping the **same device name and number**. That would explain why `list_devices.py` looked identical with and without headphones.

- If your headphones **have a small built-in mic** (a single plug with 3 dark rings, like phone earbuds), Windows may now be recording *that* mic, which may be far from your mouth or poor quality.
- If they **have no mic**, the jack input may be recording *nothing*, which gives silence.

If I've got the run order right, the mic test that worked (peak 0.055) was done **without** headphones, and Test B **with** them. That fits this explanation, but it's still a hypothesis.

```
- `resample()`: the input array's dtype should be float32, float64, int16, or int32. Input that isn't a NumPy array is converted to float32.
```

## M2, sub-step 1: convert 48 kHz stereo → 16 kHz mono

**Why it's needed:** your devices deliver 48,000 samples per second on 2 channels, but both Silero VAD and Whisper expect **16,000 samples per second, mono**. This conversion sits between capture and everything else.

**It's two operations:**
1. **Stereo → mono:** average the two channels. That's simple maths, with no library needed.
2. **48 kHz → 16 kHz (resampling):** not just "keep every third sample". Sound above 8 kHz has to be filtered out first, otherwise it folds back into the speech range as distortion. That folding is called **aliasing**.

**One subtlety:** audio arrives in 10 ms blocks. If each block were resampled separately, the filter would make a small error at every block edge (it needs a few neighbouring samples), and you'd hear faint clicks 100 times per second. So we need a **streaming resampler** that remembers the end of the previous block.

### Options

| Option | New install? | Quality | Streaming? | Code simplicity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A: `soxr`** (python binding of the libsoxr resampler) | Yes, one small package | High (`quality='HQ'` default) | ✅ `ResampleStream(48000, 16000, num_channels=1)` + `resample_chunk(x)` | ⭐ Very simple |
| B: PyAV (`av`), already installed for faster-whisper | No | High (FFmpeg's resampler) | ✅ `AudioResampler` | More complex: audio must be wrapped in "frame" objects |
| C: plain numpy (average every 3 samples) | No | Lower: weak filter, some aliasing | Works per block, since 48k/16k is exactly 3 | Simple, but lower quality |
| D: `scipy.signal.resample_poly` | Yes, large (~40 MB) | High | ❌ No memory between blocks | Simple, but wrong for streaming |

**I recommend A (`soxr`).** It's the most readable code, the streaming design is exactly what we need, and the documentation is clear. B would be my second choice, because it avoids an install, but the code would be harder for you to explain in the interview. **C** stays as a documented "simplest" alternative.

### One risk I want to test, not assume

Your mic reports **2 channels**, probably two small mics. On some laptops, one mic channel is **inverted** (a mirror image of the other). Averaging an inverted pair can **cancel out the voice**. So the test will print the level of the **left channel, the right channel and the mono mix** separately. If the mono level is much lower than either channel, we've found an inversion, and we'd use one channel instead.

### What I'd create (after the install)

- **`hylive/audio_convert.py`** (about 30 lines): `to_mono_float32(data, channels)` turns raw 16-bit stereo into mono float numbers between -1 and 1, and a small `Resampler` class wraps `soxr.ResampleStream`.
- **`scripts/convert_test.py`**: converts a WAV file **you already recorded** (e.g. `20261023-182923_mic.wav`) in 10 ms blocks, exactly as live audio would arrive. It writes `..._16k.wav` so you can listen, and prints the left/right/mono levels and the durations before and after. **No new recording is needed.**

### Approval steps

1. **Install** (you run it):

   ```powershell
   .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install soxr
   ```

   Then we pin the version it installs in `requirements.txt`.
2. I create the two files above, and you run the test.

Pass last=True once, on the final block, to flush what is left.\"\"\"\n        return self._stream.resample_chunk(mono.astype(np.float32), last=last)\nEOF\ncat > scripts/convert_test.py <<'EOF'\n\"\"\"Convert a recorded WAV to 16 kHz mono in 10 ms blocks, like live audio (milestone M2).\n\nWrites <name>_16k.wav next to the input (git-ignored) and prints levels per channel,\nso we can see whether averaging the two mic channels cancels the voice.\n\nRun from the project folder, e.g.:\n    .\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe scripts\\\\convert_test.py recordings\\\\20261023-182923_mic.wav\n\"\"\"\n\nimport argparse\nimport sys\nimport wave\nfrom pathlib import Path\n\nimport numpy as np\n\nPROJECT_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent\nsys.path.insert(0, str(PROJECT_DIR))\n\nfrom hylive.audio_convert import TARGET_RATE, Resampler, to_float32_frames, to_mono  # noqa: E402\n\nBLOCK_FRAMES = 480  # same block size as live capture (10 ms at 48 kHz)\n\n\ndef level(x: np.ndarray) -> str:\n    return f\"peak {np.abs(x).max():.3f}, RMS {np.sqrt(np.mean(x ** 2)):.4f}\"\n\n\ndef main() -> None:\n    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()\n    parser.add_argument(\"wav\", type=Path, help=\"a WAV file from recordings/\")\n    args = parser.parse_args()\n\n    with wave.open(str(args.wav), \"rb\") as wav:\n        if wav.getsampwidth() != 2:\n            raise ValueError(\"Expected a 16-bit WAV file (as written by record_test.py).\")\n        channels, in_rate = wav.getnchannels(), wav.getframerate()\n        data = wav.readframes(wav.getnframes())\n\n    frames = to_float32_frames(data, channels)\n    if len(frames) == 0:\n        raise ValueError(f\"{args.wav} contains no audio.\")\n    print(f\"input:  {args.wav.name}: {len(frames) / in_rate:.2f} s, {in_rate} Hz, {channels} ch\")\n\n    # Levels per channel and after averaging (RMS = average loudness, peak = loudest sample).\n    for ch in range(channels):\n        print(f\"  channel {ch}: {level(frames[:, ch])}\")\n    mono_full = to_mono(frames)\n    print(f\"  mono mix:  {level(mono_full)}\")\n    if channels == 2:\n        corr = np.corrcoef(frames[:, 0], frames[:, 1])[0, 1]\n        print(f\"  channel correlation: {corr:+.2f}  (+1 = identical, 0 = unrelated, -1 = inverted -> voice cancels in the mix)\")\n\n    # ## What I created

**`hylive/audio_convert.py`**: the reusable conversion module, about 35 lines.
- `to_float32_frames(data, channels)` turns raw 16-bit bytes into decimal numbers between -1 and 1, arranged as rows of `(left, right)`.
- `to_mono(frames)` averages the channels.
- `Resampler` wraps `soxr.ResampleStream(48000 → 16000)`. Its `process(block, last=False)` resamples one block and remembers where the previous block ended. `last=True` on the final block flushes the remaining audio.

**`scripts/convert_test.py`**: an offline test using recordings you already have.
1. Reads a WAV file. It **refuses** anything other than 16-bit, and refuses empty files, with a clear error.
2. Prints the **level of each channel** and of the **mono mix**, plus the **correlation** between the channels:
   - +1 means the two mics hear the same thing;
   - -1 means one is inverted, so the voice cancels in the mix.
3. Converts the file **in 10 ms blocks**, exactly as live audio will arrive, and writes `<name>_16k.wav` next to it. Git ignores it.
4. Prints the output duration and level.

## Run it

First pin the `soxr` version you installed:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip freeze | Set-Content -Encoding ascii requirements.txt
Select-String -Path requirements.txt -Pattern "soxr"
```

Then convert three of your existing recordings: the laptop mic, the headset mic, and the video.

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\convert_test.py recordings\20261023-182923_mic.wav
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\convert_test.py recordings\20261023-190138_mic.wav
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\convert_test.py recordings\20261023-190138_system.wav
```

## What to check

**In the printed output:**
- The **output duration equals the input duration** (for example 15.00 s → 15.00 s). That proves no audio was lost or duplicated at block edges.
- **Mono mix level vs. channel levels:** the mono RMS should be about the same as the channels, not much lower.
- **Correlation:** a value close to **+1** is good. A value near **-1** would mean the voice cancels, and we'd switch to using one channel.

**By listening** to the three `_16k.wav` files: they should sound like the originals, only slightly less crisp, since 16 kHz cuts the highest frequencies. There should be **no clicking, crackling or robotic sound**. Clicks would mean the block edges are wrong.

Paste all four outputs (`Select-String` plus the three conversions) and your listening impression.

```
def get_vad_model():
    """Returns the VAD model instance."""
    path = os.path.join(get_assets_path(), "silero_vad_v6.onnx")
    return SileroVADModel(path)


class SileroVADModel:
    def __init__(self, path):
        try:
            import onnxruntime
        except ImportError as e:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "Applying the VAD filter requires the onnxruntime package"
            ) from e

        opts = onnxruntime.SessionOptions()
        opts.inter_op_num_threads = 1
        opts.intra_op_num_threads = 1
        opts.enable_cpu_mem_arena = False
        opts.log_severity_level = 4

        self.session = onnxruntime.InferenceSession(
            path,
            providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"],
            sess_options=opts,
        )

    def __call__(
        self, audio: np.ndarray, num_samples: int = 512, context_size_samples: int = 64
    ):
        assert audio.ndim == 1, "Input should be a 1D array"
        assert (
            audio.shape[0] % num_samples == 0
        ), "Input size should be a multiple of num_samples"

        h = np.zeros((1, 1, 128), dtype="float32")
        c = np.zeros((1, 1, 128), dtype="float32")
        context = np.zeros(
            (1, context_size_samples),
            dtype="float32",
        )

        batched_audio = audio.reshape(-1, num_samples)
        context = batched_audio[..., -context_size_samples:]
        context[-1] = 0
        context = np.roll(context, 1, 0)
        batched_audio = np.concatenate([context, batched_audio], 1)

        batched_audio = batched_audio.reshape(-1, num_samples + context_size_samples)

        encoder_batch_size = 10000
        num_segments = batched_audio.shape[0]
        outputs = []
        for i in range(0, num_segments, encoder_batch_size):
            output, h, c = self.session.run(
                None,
                {"input": batched_audio[i : i + encoder_batch_size], "h": h, "c": c},
            )
            outputs.append(output)

        out = np.concatenate(outputs, axis=0)

        return out

```

## M2, sub-step 2: voice activity detection (VAD)

### What it does, simply

The mic delivers a continuous stream of audio, but Whisper needs **one phrase at a time**. VAD is a small neural network that looks at the audio in **32 ms windows** (512 samples at 16 kHz) and outputs the **probability that someone is speaking** in each window. On top of that, we build a **segmenter**:

- Speech probability goes **above** a threshold → a phrase **starts**.
- It stays **below** the threshold for a set **silence time** (e.g. 0.5 s) → the phrase **ends**. The audio from start to end is sent to Whisper.
- **Maximum phrase length** (e.g. 10–15 s): if someone talks without pausing, we cut anyway, otherwise the 5-second latency rule breaks.

**The key trade-off:** a **shorter silence time** means lower latency, but it can cut sentences in the middle when people pause briefly. A **longer** one keeps sentences whole but adds delay. We'll tune it by measurement in M2/M3.

VAD also solves the "A-A-A-A…" problem from D-009: **non-speech never reaches Whisper.**

### Options (checked just now)

| Option | Install | Streaming support | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A: official `silero-vad` 6.2.3** (released Sep 23, 2026) | Requires **`torch`** (CPU), roughly 200–300 MB | ✅ Documented `VADIterator`, fed 512-sample windows one by one | Larger install. But we **need CPU torch anyway in M5** for the speaker-embedding model (D-002), so it isn't wasted |
| B: the Silero model **bundled inside faster-whisper** (`silero_vad_v6.onnx`) | None | ❌ Its wrapper is built for whole files. I read the installed code: it's a custom export with internal inputs (`h`, `c`) | We'd rely on an **internal, undocumented** part of another library, which could break on any update |
| C: `webrtcvad` | Small | Yes | An older approach, generally less accurate on noisy audio |

**I recommend A.** It's the official, maintained, documented streaming API, and the torch dependency is one we'll need anyway. B is tempting because nothing needs installing, but it breaks our "verify, don't rely on undocumented things" rule. Honestly, though: the wiki page I read **doesn't fully document `VADIterator`'s settings and return values**, so I'll read the installed source after the install to confirm them before writing code.

### Things we'll verify after installing

- **torch must be the CPU version.** On Windows, the PyPI torch package is normally CPU-only, but we'll **check it** (`torch.version.cuda` should print `None`), in line with D-002.
- **RAM:** torch takes a few hundred MB once imported. We'll keep an eye on it, given your 8 GB.

### Approval step: install (you run it)

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --no-cache-dir silero-vad==6.2.3
```

Then verify:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -c "import torch, silero_vad; print('torch', torch.__version__, '| cuda build:', torch.version.cuda)"
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip show silero-vad
```

**Expected:** `cuda build: None`, plus the package details.

**After that** (separate approval): I read the installed `VADIterator` source, explain it, and write `hylive/segmenter.py` together with a test that runs it on your `laptop_mic` recording and prints the detected phrases with start and end times.

**Time:** started at 01:41. This install-and-verify step takes about 10 minutes. Shall I go ahead (you run the install)?

I've read the installed `VADIterator` source, so I can now describe exactly what it does.

## What `VADIterator` actually does (from the installed code)

- You feed it **one window of exactly 512 samples** (32 ms at 16 kHz) per call. It returns:
  - `{'start': n}` when speech begins, where `n` is the sample position, already moved back slightly by the padding;
  - `{'end': n}` when the silence has lasted long enough;
  - `None` the rest of the time.
- **Thresholds:** speech "starts" when the probability is **≥ 0.5**, and only "ends" when it drops **below 0.35** (0.5 - 0.15). Two different thresholds keep it from flickering on and off at the boundary. This is called **hysteresis**.
- **Default silence time: only 100 ms.** That's fine for detecting words, but **too short for phrases**: it would split a sentence at every small pause. We'll set it ourselves, starting at **500 ms**.
- **There's no maximum phrase length.** We have to add that ourselves, otherwise one long monologue would only be printed when the speaker stops.

## Proposed design

**`hylive/segmenter.py`**, about 70 lines:

- **Output:** `Segment(source, audio, start_s, end_s, ended_at)`, matching `PLAN.md`:
  - `audio` is the phrase as 16 kHz mono;
  - `start_s` / `end_s` are its position in the session, used for the `[00:01:12]` timestamp;
  - `ended_at` is the clock time when the end was detected, which is the starting point of the **5-second latency measurement**.
- **`Segmenter.process(samples)`** receives audio in any block size (our blocks are 10 ms = 160 samples), collects it into 512-sample windows for the VAD, and returns the finished segments.
- **Memory:** it keeps only the current phrase plus a short **pre-roll** (0.3 s before the start), not the whole session. A one-hour call would otherwise use hundreds of MB.
- **Settings**, as constructor arguments with clear defaults, to tune later:
  - `min_silence_ms=500`;
  - `max_segment_s=10`: when a phrase reaches 10 s, it's cut and sent, and the rest continues as a new segment;
  - `speech_pad_ms=100`: a little audio kept before and after, so first and last syllables aren't clipped;
  - `threshold=0.5`.
- **D-010** (loopback silence) isn't relevant yet, since the mic always delivers data. I'll leave a comment pointing to it for M5.

**`scripts/vad_test.py <wav>`** runs on your existing recordings:
1. Reads the WAV, then converts and feeds it **in 10 ms blocks**, exactly like live capture, through `audio_convert` and then the segmenter.
2. Prints each detected phrase: number, start, end, duration.
3. Saves each phrase as its own small WAV in `recordings/segments/` (ignored by Git), so **you can listen and check** whether phrases start and end in the right places.
4. Has optional flags `--min-silence-ms` and `--max-segment-s`, so we can compare settings without editing code.

**Test plan:**
1. `laptop_mic`: phrases should match what you said, with pauses skipped.
2. `headset_mic` (very quiet): does VAD still find speech? Either answer is useful information.

Silero VAD requires exactly 512 samples per call at 16 kHz\n\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Segment:\n    source: str          # \"mic\" or \"system\"\n    audio: np.ndarray    # 16 kHz mono float32\n    start_s: float       # position in the stream (seconds since the stream started)\n    end_s: float\n    ended_at: float      # clock time when the end was detected (start of the latency measurement)\n\n\ndef load_vad_model():\n    return load_silero_vad()\n\n\nclass Segmenter:\n    def __init__(self, source: str, model, threshold: float = 0.5, min_silence_ms: int = 500,\n                 speech_pad_ms: int = 100, max_segment_s: float = 10.0, preroll_s: float = 0.3):\n        self.source = source\n        self._vad = VADIterator(model, threshold=threshold, sampling_rate=SAMPLE_RATE,\n                                min_silence_duration_ms=min_silence_ms, speech_pad_ms=speech_pad_ms)\n        self._max_samples = int(max_segment_s * SAMPLE_RATE)\n        self._preroll = int(preroll_s * SAMPLE_RATE)  #
