stream sample index where the phrase started; None = silence\n\n    def process(self, samples: np.ndarray, now: float | None = None) -> list[Segment]:\n        \"\"\"Add audio; return the phrases that ended in it (often an empty list).\"\"\"\n        now = time.monotonic() if now is None else now\n        self._pending = np.concatenate([self._pending, samples.astype(np.float32)])\n        segments = []\n        while len(self._pending) >= VAD_WINDOW:\n            window = self._pending[:VAD_WINDOW]\n            self._pending = self._pending[VAD_WINDOW:]\n            self._buffer = np.concatenate([self._buffer, window])\n            self._fed += VAD_WINDOW\n\n            event = self._vad(torch.from_numpy(window))\n            if event and \"start\" in event:\n                self._seg_start = max(event[\"start\"], self._buffer_start)\n            elif event and \"end\" in event:\n                end = min(event[\"end\"], self._fed)\n                if end > self._seg_start:  # still speaking: the rest becomes the next segment\n            self._trim()\n        return segments\n\n    def flush(self, now: float | None = None) -> list[Segment]:\n        \"\"\"End of stream: return the unfinished phrase, if any.\"\"\"\n        now = time.monotonic() if now is None else now\n        if self._seg_start is None or self._fed <= self._seg_start:\n            return []\n        segment = self._cut(self._fed, now)\n        self._seg_start = None\n        return [segment]\n\n    def _cut(self, end: int, now: float) -> Segment:\n        audio = self._buffer[self._seg_start - self._buffer_start:end - self._buffer_start].copy()\n        return Segment(self.source, audio, self._seg_start / SAMPLE_RATE, end / SAMPLE_RATE, now)\n\n    def _trim(self) -> None:\n        \"\"\"Drop audio we no longer need: keep the current phrase, or only the pre-roll during silence.\"\"\"\n        keep_from = self._seg_start if self._seg_start is not None else self._fed - self._preroll\n        drop = keep_from - self._buffer_start\n        if drop > 0:\n            self._buffer = self._buffer[drop:]\n            self._buffer_start = keep_from\nEOF\ncat > scripts/vad_test.py <<'EOF'\n\"\"\"Run the VAD segmenter on a recorded WAV, fed in 10 ms blocks like live audio (milestone M2).\n\nPrints each detected phrase and saves it as a WAV in recordings/segments/<file name>/ (git-ignored).\n\"Detected after\" = how long after the end of the phrase the segmenter reported it\n(this delay counts towards the 5-second latency budget).\n\nRun from the project folder, e.g.:\n    .\\\\.venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe scripts\\\\vad_test.py recordings\\\\20261023-193822_laptop_mic.wav\n\"\"\"\n\nimport argparse\nimport sys\nimport time\nimport wave\nfrom pathlib import Path\n\nimport numpy as np\n\nPROJECT_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent\nsys.path.insert(0, str(PROJECT_DIR))\n\nfrom hylive.audio_convert import TARGET_RATE, Resampler, to_float32_frames, to_mono  # noqa: E402\nfrom hylive.segmenter import Segmenter, load_vad_model  # noqa: E402\n\nBLOCK_SECONDS = 0.010  # live capture delivers 10 ms blocks\n\n\ndef write_wav(path: Path, audio: np.ndarray) -> None:\n    with wave.open(str(path), \"wb\") as wav:\n        wav.setnchannels(1)\n        wav.setsampwidth(2)\n        wav.setframerate(TARGET_RATE)\n        wav.writeframes((np.clip(audio, -1.0, 1.0) * 32767).astype(np.int16).tobytes())\n\n\ndef main() -> None:\n    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()\n    parser.add_argument(\"wav\", type=Path)\n    parser.add_argument(\"--threshold\", type=float, default=0.5)\n    parser.add_argument(\"--min-silence-ms\", type=int, default=500)\n    parser.add_argument(\"--max-segment-s\", type=float, default=10.0)\n    args = parser.parse_args()\n\n    with wave.open(str(args.wav), \"rb\") as wav:\n        if wav.getsampwidth() != 2:\n            raise ValueError(\"Expected a 16-bit WAV file (as written by record_test.py).\")\n        channels, in_rate = wav.getnchannels(), wav.getframerate()\n        frames = to_float32_frames(wav.readframes(wav.getnframes()), channels)\n    if len(frames) == 0:\n        raise ValueError(f\"{args.wav} contains no audio.\")\n\n    model = load_vad_model()\n    segmenter = Segmenter(\"mic\", model, threshold=args.threshold,\n                          min_silence_ms=args.min_silence_ms, max_segment_s=args.max_segment_s)\n    resampler = Resampler(in_rate)\n    block = int(in_rate * BLOCK_SECONDS)\n    starts = range(0, len(frames), block)\n\n    segments = []\n    t0 = time.perf_counter()\n    for i, start in enumerate(starts):\n        audio16k = resampler.process(to_mono(frames[start:start + block]), last=(i == len(starts) - 1))\n        stream_time = (start + block) / in_rate  # simulated \"now\": how much audio has arrived so far\n        segments += segmenter.process(audio16k, now=stream_time)\n    segments += segmenter.flush(now=len(frames) / in_rate)\n    processing = time.perf_counter() - t0\n\n    out_dir = PROJECT_DIR / \"recordings\" / \"segments\" / args.wav.stem\n    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)\n    total = len(frames) / in_rate\n    print(f\"{args.wav.name}: {total:.2f} s | threshold {args.threshold}, min silence \"\n          f\"{args.min_silence_ms} ms, max segment {args.max_segment_s} s\\n\")\n    print(f\"{'#':>3}  {'start':>6}  {'end':>6}  {'dur':>5}  {'detected after':>14}  file\")\n    for n, seg in enumerate(segments, 1):\n        path = out_dir / f\"seg{n:02d}.wav\"\n        write_wav(path, seg.audio)\n        print(f\"{n:>3}  {seg.start_s:6.2f}  {seg.end_s:6.2f}  {seg.end_s - seg.start_s:5.2f}  \"\n              f\"{seg.ended_at - seg.end_s:13.2f}s  {path.relative_to(PROJECT_DIR)}\")\n    speech = sum(seg.end_s - seg.start_s for seg in segments)\n    print(f\"\\n{len(segments)} phrases, {speech:.1f} s of speech in {total:.1f} s of audio\")\n    print(f\"processing time {processing:.2f} s ({processing / total:.3f} s per second of audio)\")\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    main()\nEOF\nfor f in hylive/segmenter.py scripts/vad_test.py; do python3 -c \"import ast,sys;ast.parse(open(sys.argv[1]).read());print(sys.argv[1],'syntax OK')\" $f; done; grep -n \"silero\\|torch\" requirements.txt"

## `hylive/segmenter.py`: how it works

**`Segmenter.process(samples)`** is called with every 10 ms block (160 samples at 16 kHz):

1. It adds the samples to `_pending` and, whenever **512** have collected, passes one window to Silero's `VADIterator`.
2. On a **`start`** event, it remembers where the phrase began.
3. On an **`end`** event, it cuts the phrase's audio out of the buffer and returns a `Segment`.
4. **Max length:** if a phrase reaches **10 s**, it's cut and returned immediately, and the rest continues as the next segment.
5. **`_trim()`** keeps memory small. During silence, only the last 0.3 s is kept (the pre-roll); during speech, only the current phrase.

There's also **`flush()`**, for when a recording ends in the middle of a phrase.

**One edge case is handled on purpose,** with a comment explaining it. Right after a max-length cut, the VAD's `end` position can fall *before* the cut, because of its padding. Then there's nothing left to emit, so nothing is emitted. That isn't hiding an error; it's simply an empty phrase.

## `scripts/vad_test.py`: what it prints

For each detected phrase:
- **start / end / duration**, in seconds into the recording;
- **"detected after"**: how long after the phrase ended the segmenter noticed. This counts towards the 5-second budget, and should be roughly the silence setting (0.5 s);
- the saved file: `recordings\segments\<recording name>\seg01.wav`, `seg02.wav` and so on.

Plus a summary: the number of phrases, the seconds of speech, and the **processing time per second of audio**, which shows whether VAD is fast enough to run live.

## Run it

**Test 1: laptop mic** (clear speech):

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\vad_test.py recordings\20261023-193822_laptop_mic.wav
```

**Test 2: headset mic** (very quiet speech):

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\vad_test.py recordings\20261023-194557_headset_mic.wav
```

**What to check:**
- **The number of phrases** should match roughly how many sentences or pauses you remember. **Listen to a few `segXX.wav` files:** does each start and end cleanly, without cut-off first or last syllables?
- **"Detected after"** should be about **0.5 s**.
- **Processing time** should be well below **1 s per second of audio**, otherwise VAD couldn't keep up live.
- **Headset test:** does it find speech at all? Both answers are useful.

On the first run, `silero_vad` loads its model, which takes a second or two. Paste both outputs.

What this tells us:

- **It segments speech.** Two phrases per recording, with the pauses at the start, in the middle and at the end skipped. Please **listen to the four `seg01`/`seg02` files** to confirm that they match what you said and that no first or last syllables are cut off.
- **End detection takes about 0.47 s**, consistent with the 500 ms silence setting. So **about 0.5 s of our 5-second budget** goes to deciding that a phrase has ended. That leaves about 4.5 s for transcription and translation. Good margin so far.
- **Fast enough for live use.** The first run's 0.144 s per second includes one-time model loading; the second run shows the real cost, about 3% of real time. VAD won't be a bottleneck.
- **VAD even detects the very quiet headset speech.** Silero looks at the *pattern* of speech, not only the loudness. That doesn't mean Whisper will understand it, though, so the headset decision (D-012) still stands.

**About the warning:** `torch.jit.load is deprecated` is a *FutureWarning*. It means "this will be removed in a future torch version", not that anything is wrong now. It comes from inside `silero_vad`, from loading its default model format. Silero also offers an **ONNX version** of the same model (`load_silero_vad(onnx=True)`) that doesn't use `torch.jit`, and the `onnxruntime` it needs is already installed. I'd note it as a possible later cleanup, **not change it now**, since what we have works and has been tested.

## M2, sub-step 3: transcription (design, for approval)

**Goal:** send each phrase from the segmenter to Whisper and get Armenian text. This is the **first real speed test with speech**.

**Starting model: Whisper "small".** It's not a final choice: M3 compares models with numbers. "small" is a sensible start because it's fast and fits easily in 3 GB of VRAM. It's about a 480 MB download, saved into `models/`, which Git ignores. Smaller models are usually noticeably worse at Armenian, so **expect mediocre text**. Tonight's goal is the plumbing and the timing, not the final quality.

**New files:**
- **`hylive/gpu.py`**: the NVIDIA DLL registration from the smoke test, moved into a reusable function. Every program that uses the GPU needs it.
- **`hylive/asr.py`**: a small `Transcriber` class. It loads the model once and does a **warm-up run** at start (D-009, so the first real phrase isn't the slow one). Its `transcribe(audio)` returns the Armenian text. Settings:
  - `language="hy"`;
  - `temperature=0.0`, so no hidden retries (D-009);
  - `int8_float32`, our verified GPU type;

**Speed is excellent:**

| | Time |
|---|---|

That's plenty of room. With about 0.5 s for end detection plus about 0.5 s for transcription, we're at about 1 s of the 5-second budget, before translation.

**Quality is poor, as expected for "small":**

| | Text |
|---|---|
| You said | Բարև, ես հիմա փորձարկում եմ իմ խոսափողը, համակարգչով ոչինչ միացված չէ |

| **CER** (wrong characters) | **43%** |
| **WER** (wrong words) | **91%** (10 of 11 words wrong) |

The output *sounds* similar (համակարկչով for համակարգչով, հապողը for խոսափողը), but it's mostly the wrong words. A translator would produce nonsense from this. This confirms the warning in the brief: Armenian is low-resource, and small models aren't good enough.

## Comparison against what you said

| | small | **medium** |
|---|---|---|
| Phrase 1 | ոալեվ իման որ չարկով եմ հոս հապողը | **բարև, ես** իմաբոր ձերկովերուն հոսապողը |
| Phrase 2 | Համակարկչովոթինչ միանց հասջյվ | համաքարհհչշով **ոչինչ** միածհաստյեն |
| **CER** (wrong characters) | 43% | **37%** |
| **WER** (wrong words) | 91% | **73%** |
| Time per phrase | about 0.5 s | **about 1.1 s** |

Medium is better (it gets "բարև, ես" and "ոչինչ" right), but 73% wrong words is still not usable for translation. On the positive side, speed is no problem.

**An important pattern in the timings:** both phrases took almost the same time (1.07 s and 1.09 s), even though one is 40% longer. That's how Whisper works: it always processes a **fixed 30-second window**, so the cost per phrase is roughly **constant**, whatever its length. That's good news for larger models. Their time per phrase will be higher, but it won't explode with long phrases.

## My recommendation

**1. Test large-v3 once, right now** (about 3 GB download plus one run, roughly 10–15 minutes). It's the best general Whisper model for low-resource languages, and we have speed to spare. A rough estimate is 2–3 s per phrase, but **that's a guess, not a fact**. I'll set the decision rule **before** we see the result, so we don't rationalise afterwards:

- If large-v3 fits in VRAM, takes **≤ 3 s per phrase** and is **clearly better** (CER noticeably below 37%), it becomes our baseline.
- Otherwise we keep **medium** as the baseline and move on.
- Either way, **model testing stops here for now.** One sentence isn't enough for a final decision. M3 gets **one capped block (≤ 1.5 h)** later, on a proper 10-sentence evaluation set, plus at most one community Armenian fine-tune and a beam-size check.

**2. Then, tonight: translation + the live mic-only program.** That completes M2, the walking skeleton: you speak, and Armenian plus English lines appear in the terminal with measured latency. That's the biggest step towards a working application. Translation uses NLLB-200 through CTranslate2, which I'll verify before installing.

**NLLB section**

The page describes NLLB as "a collection of multilingual models trained by Meta and supporting 200 languages." The example uses the smallest version, which has 600M parameters.

**Required packages**

- The general converter setup, from the Transformers intro, is `pip install transformers[torch]`, followed by running `ct2-transformers-converter` with a model name or model directory path.
- For NLLB specifically, the page says: "Converting NLLB models requires `transformers>=4.21.0`."

**Conversion command**

```
ct2-transformers-converter --model facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M --output_dir nllb-200-distilled-600M
```

**Translation example**

```
import ctranslate2
import transformers

src_lang = "eng_Latn"
tgt_lang = "fra_Latn"

translator = ctranslate2.Translator("nllb-200-distilled-600M")
tokenizer = transformers.AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M", src_lang=src_lang)

source = tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(tokenizer.encode("Hello world!"))
target_prefix = [tgt_lang]
results = translator.translate_batch([source], target_prefix=[target_prefix])
target = results[0].hypotheses[0][1:]

print(tokenizer.decode(tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(target)))
```

The example sets the source language on the tokenizer, converts the input text to tokens, and passes the target language code as the `target_prefix`. It then drops the first token from the first hypothesis and converts the remaining tokens back to IDs before decoding them to text.

## large-v3 result: it passes the decision rule ✅

| | small | medium | **large-v3** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phrase 1 | ոալեվ իման որ չարկով եմ հոս հապողը | բարև, ես իմաբոր ձերկովերուն հոսապողը | **Վարև, ես իմ ապործարկում եմ խոսապողը** |
| Phrase 2 | Համակարկչովոթինչ միանց հասջյվ | համաքարհհչշով ոչինչ միածհաստյեն | **համակարգթյով ոչինք միածված չէ** |
| **CER** | 43% | 37% | **21%** |
| WER | 91% | 73% | 73% |
| Time per phrase | ~0.5 s | ~1.1 s | **~1.8 s** |
| Fits in 3 GB VRAM | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

- **CER fell from 37% to 21%:** clearly better, as the rule required. Most words are now **one or two letters off** (Վարև/Բարև, խոսապողը/խոսափողը, միածված/միացված). That's why WER stays at 73%: WER counts a word with one wrong letter as completely wrong. CER is the fairer measure here, and the text is now **readable** for an Armenian speaker. A translation model may cope with small spelling errors like these, which is what we'll check next.
- **About 1.8 s per phrase, well under 3 s.** Latency estimate: 0.5 s end detection + 1.8 s ASR + translation ≈ 2.5–3 s. That's within 5 s, with one caveat for M6: if you and a remote speaker finish at the same moment, the second phrase waits for the GPU (about +1.8 s).
- Loading took 195 s **including the 3 GB download**. Later starts will be much faster; we'll measure that.

**Decision: large-v3 is the ASR baseline.** Model testing pauses until M3, which is capped at 1.5 h.

## Important fix for the conversion step: keep the 2.5 GB download off C:

The converter downloads the original NLLB model through Hugging Face, and **by default that goes to `C:\Users\User\.cache`**. That's your nearly full drive, and it would break D-004. Setting `HF_HOME` sends it into the project's `models\` folder instead. The setting only lasts for the current PowerShell window; nothing changes system-wide.

## Commands (in order, in the same PowerShell window)

**1. Install transformers:**

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --no-cache-dir "transformers>=4.21.0"
```

**2. Convert NLLB to CTranslate2 int8**, with the download kept on D:

```powershell
$env:HF_HOME = "D:\Em\mathrix\models\hf_home"
.\.venv\Scripts\ct2-transformers-converter.exe --model facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M --output_dir models\nllb-200-distilled-600M-ct2-int8 --quantization int8
```

**Expected:** download progress, then it finishes without errors. The output folder `models\nllb-200-distilled-600M-ct2-int8` should contain a `model.bin` of roughly 600 MB.

**3. Run the translation test:**

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\mt_test.py
```

## What the new code does

**`hylive/translate.py`**: the `Translator` class.
- It registers the NVIDIA DLLs first, keeping the same import order as everywhere else.
- It **refuses to start** with a clear message if the converted model is missing.
- It loads the CTranslate2 model (CPU, int8 by default) and the NLLB tokenizer, with the tokenizer cached in `models\`. The source language is Armenian (`hye_Armn`).
- `translate(text)` follows the official guide's example exactly: split into tokens, translate with `target_prefix = eng_Latn`, drop the language-code token, convert back to text. Empty text returns an empty string.

**`scripts/mt_test.py`** loads and warms up the model, then translates 5 sentences with the time for each:
- **both of your phrases twice**: the correct version, and large-v3's misspelled version. This shows how much the ASR errors hurt the English.
- the brief's example, "Բարև, ինչպե՞ս ես։".

It has a `--device cuda` flag, for a GPU comparison if the CPU turns out too slow.

**If anything fails, paste the full output.** Possible issues include a missing tokenizer package (for example `sentencepiece`) or a converter error. I won't guess at fixes before seeing the message.

## What I built

**`hylive/__main__.py`** is the program itself, started with `python -m hylive`. It runs three parts in parallel:

| Part | Job | Module |
|---|---|---|
| PortAudio callback | Records the mic in 10 ms blocks into the **audio queue** | `audio_capture` |
| **Thread 1: segmentation** | Converts to 16 kHz mono, runs VAD, puts finished phrases into the **phrase queue** | `audio_convert`, `segmenter` |
| **Thread 2: processing** | Whisper → NLLB → prints the result | `asr`, `translate` |

**Why two threads:** segmentation must keep up with the live audio at all times, while transcription takes about 2 s per phrase. If both ran in one loop, audio would pile up while Whisper works. This way you can keep speaking, and new phrases simply queue up.

**What it prints per phrase:**

```
[00:00:05] Me
HY: ...
EN: ...
    latency 2.7 s (ASR 1.8 s, translation 0.5 s, queue 0)
```

The latency follows **the brief's definition**: from the end of the spoken phrase to the English line. A code comment notes that it's an approximation, ignoring tiny driver buffering. `queue` shows how many phrases are waiting; anything above 0 means it's falling behind.

**Other behaviour:**
- `--list-devices` prints the recordable devices (R1-1, now in the main program).
- `--mic N`, or the Windows default mic, printed either way.
- `--asr-model` defaults to large-v3. The VAD settings can be changed with flags.
- All models are loaded and **warmed up before** it says "Ready", so your first sentence isn't slow.
- **Ctrl+C** stops capture and finishes the last phrase before exiting.
- **If a thread crashes, the program stops with the full error.** It doesn't keep running silently with a dead thread.

I also added `recordable_devices()` at the end of `audio_capture.py`. Nothing existing was changed.

## 1. Shutdown bug: confirmed

Look at the order of the output:

```
Stopping: finishing the last phrase ...
phrases detected: 2 (of which 0 at shutdown), printed: 1   ← main thread already finished
problem flags from PortAudio: 0 blocks
[00:00:08] Me                                             ← phrase 2 printed AFTER that
```

The main thread is supposed to **wait** until the processing thread has printed everything. Here it didn't wait: it printed the summary and started exiting while phrase 2 was still being transcribed. **This time phrase 2 got printed just in time, before Python closed. In your first run, it probably didn't**, because when the main program exits, Python kills the background threads mid-work. That would explain the lost sentences at 03:31. The counters did their job.

**Likely cause:** the main thread waits using `thread.join()` / `is_alive()`, and pressing Ctrl+C *during* `join()` can leave Python's thread bookkeeping in a wrong state. I believe this is a known CPython issue in versions like your 3.12.1, but **I'm not 100% sure of the exact cause**. That's why I'd make a fix that works whatever the cause.

**Proposed fix (about 10 lines):** the processing thread sets a `threading.Event` called "done" when it has truly finished, and the main thread waits on that event instead of using `join()`/`is_alive()`. An event is a simple flag that one thread raises and another waits for; it isn't affected by Ctrl+C in this way. The counters stay, so the next test proves whether the fix works.

## 2. Latency: close to the limit when sentences run together

| | Phrase 1 | Phrase 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Content | **two sentences merged** (pause shorter than 0.5 s) | one sentence |
| ASR | **3.0 s** | 1.6 s |
| Translation | 0.9 s | 0.7 s |
| **Latency** | **4.8 s** ⚠️ | 3.2 s |

My earlier statement that time per phrase is "roughly constant" was **only partly true**. The 30-second window costs the same each time, but **producing the text takes longer when there are more words**. So longer phrases take longer, and with `max_segment_s=10` a long monologue could exceed 5 s. **For M6:** probably lower the maximum phrase length to about 5–6 s and measure again. All four pieces are in place and syntax-checked. The text normalisation works correctly on Armenian («Բարև, ինչպե՞ս ես։» becomes «բարև ինչպես ես», with the ՞ and ։ removed), and `eval/audio/` is ignored by Git.

## What was created or changed

- **`eval/sentences.txt`**: the 10 sentences you approved, one per line (`01<tab>sentence`). This file gets committed.
- **`hylive/asr.py`**: one small addition. `Transcriber` accepts an optional `initial_prompt`, which is passed to Whisper. The default is `None`, so the live program behaves exactly as before.
- **`scripts/record_eval.py`**: for each sentence it shows the text, waits for **Enter**, records 6 s, and saves `eval/audio/evalNN.wav`. It prints the peak level, and if a recording is quieter than 0.02 it **flags it visibly** with the command to re-record it (`--only NN`).
- **`scripts/eval_asr.py`**: sends every clip through **the same path as the live program** (mono → 16 kHz → VAD → Whisper) and prints, per sentence, the CER, the time, the number of phrases, the reference and the hypothesis. At the end it prints **one RESULT line** with the overall CER and the average and maximum ASR time.
  - Normalisation also treats «եւ» and «և» as the same, so spelling variants of that ligature aren't counted as errors.
  - The `--prompt` text («Սա հայերեն խոսակցություն է։ Մենք խոսում ենք հայերեն։», "This is an Armenian conversation. We speak Armenian.") **deliberately shares no words** with the test sentences. Otherwise it could unfairly hand Whisper the answers.

**1. Record the 10 sentences.** Headphones unplugged, nothing playing, normal distance and loudness:

Clear results, and the per-sentence lines reveal a pattern worth one more quick test.

## Results (10 sentences, large-v3)

| Setting | **CER** | ASR avg | **ASR max** | Within rule (max ≤ 2.5 s)? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **beam 1** | **8.6%** | 1.67 s | **1.89 s** | ✅ |
| beam 5 | 6.4% | 2.80 s | 3.73 s | ❌ too slow |
| beam 5 + prompt | 12.8% | 2.50 s | 3.85 s | ❌ worse *and* slower |

**Applying the rule we set in advance: beam 1 wins.**

- **Beam 5 is 2.2 points better, but too slow.** Its maximum of 3.73 s plus about 0.5 s VAD and 0.7 s translation would put latency at about 5 s. Almost all of its gain also comes from **one sentence** (07: 21.4% → 3.6%). On the others it's identical or nearly so.
- **The prompt made things worse.** On sentence 07 it **hallucinated** («3-3 անձր է վերկալիս»). That's a known Whisper risk with prompts. **Rejected.**
- **Good news overall:** 8.6% CER on clearly read sentences is **much better** than the 21% from the earlier test recording. Three sentences are perfect or almost (03 at 0%, 05 and 10 at under 3%).

## The pattern: Armenian words starting with Բ lose their first sound

| # | Should be | Whisper wrote |
|---|---|---|
| 01 | **Բ**արև | **Վ**արև |
| 04 | **Բ**ոլորը | ոլորը, with the **Բ completely missing** |
| 08 | **Բ**ժիշկը | **Վ**աժիշկը |

**3 of the 4 words starting with Բ are wrong, in every setting.** Meanwhile, Վաղը (03), which starts with Վ, is always correct. «ոլորը» (04), with the first sound *missing entirely*, is a strong hint. **I suspect the problem is our VAD cutting, not Whisper.** "Բ" starts with a short, quiet burst of sound that VAD may not yet count as speech, so the phrase starts a few milliseconds too late, and Whisper never hears the full "Բ". That's a hypothesis, and it's cheap to test.

## Proposed test (one change, one run)

**Change (needs your OK):**
- **`scripts/eval_asr.py`** gets a `--pad-ms` flag. That's the padding the segmenter keeps before (and after) each phrase; it's currently 100 ms.
- **`hylive/segmenter.py`**: the pre-roll buffer becomes at least *padding + 0.2 s*. Otherwise a larger padding can't actually reach further back, because there's no audio stored before 0.3 s. This changes **nothing** at the current 100 ms setting.

**Run:**

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\eval_asr.py --beam-size 1 --pad-ms 300
```

**Decision rule:**
- If the Բ words are fixed and CER drops by **≥ 2 points**, adopt 300 ms padding. It costs **no extra latency**, because the end of a phrase is still detected after the same 500 ms of silence.
- If not, keep 100 ms. The hypothesis is then ruled out, and the Բ problem goes into the README as a known limitation.

**Time:** 16:53, about 40 minutes of the M3 cap used, about 50 minutes left. After this test, I suggest we **close M3** (skipping the fine-tuned model search). 8.6% CER is a decent baseline, and the bigger remaining risks are the **system audio** and **speaker labels**.

May I make the two small changes?

## My reading of the 10 sentences (please confirm or correct, since you're the native speaker)

| # | EN (reference): NLLB on correct Armenian | EN (ASR): what the live program shows |
|---|---|---|
| 01 | ✅ Hi, how are you? | ❌ Wow, what do you look like? *(Բ→Վ)* |
| 02 | ✅ I'm fine, thank you. | ⚠️ Thank you very much. *(the gist only)* |
| 03 | ✅ I'm meeting my friends tomorrow. | ✅ identical |
| 04 | ✅ They're all home now. | ✅ They've already returned home. |
| 05 | ✅ We're testing the new program today. | ⚠️ This is how we test the new program. |
| 06 | ✅ Can you repeat the last sentence? | ❌ You can make the last statement. |
| 07 | ✅ It was raining last night. | ❌ It was raining about three feet. |
| 08 | ✅ The doctor will call you in the morning. | ❌ The singer will be alive tomorrow morning. |
| 09 | ✅ Our meeting was moved to the next week. | ⚠️ …moved to the next round. |
| 10 | ✅ I like to drink coffee before work. | ❌ I like to drink seriously before work. *(սուրջ for սուրճ)* |
| | **10/10 understandable** | **about 2 correct, 3 gist, 5 wrong** |

## What this means

1. **NLLB is good.** All 10 reference translations are understandable. By our rule, **no opus-mt test**: a different translator would get the same broken input.
2. **The problem is ASR → translation sensitivity.** Even a **one-letter** error can flip the meaning: «սուրջ» instead of «սուրճ» turned *coffee* into *seriously*, and «Վաժիշկը» turned *doctor* into *singer*. So an 8.6% CER doesn't mean 91% good English.
3. **Translation is fast:** about 0.4–0.5 s per sentence. ✅

## What I recommend: accept this as an honest, documented limitation for now, and move on

- **What could improve it** is a better Armenian ASR, such as a fine-tuned model, or beam 5, which costs latency. Both are uncertain and slow to test.
- **What isn't built yet** is required by the brief and *will* be tested live: **system audio** and **speaker labels** (Speaker 1 / Speaker 2), with two people on the call. If those are missing, the result fails much more visibly than imperfect English.
- If time remains at the end (the buffer, around Oct 30), the **first candidate** is retesting `beam 5` together with the shorter maximum phrase length planned for M6. The latency margin may then allow it.

**For the README**, this is exactly the kind of honest finding the brief values: *"A solution that is honest about its limits beats one that hides them."*

## Next steps (need your OK)

1. **Confirm or correct my ✅/⚠️/❌ table**. It's the R3-1 judgement, and it should be yours.
2. I record it in `TESTS.md` (R3-1, R3-2) and `DECISIONS.md` (D-016 confirmed; opus-mt "considered, not tested, because…"), plus `TIMELOG.md` and `HANDOVER.md`. Then you commit. **M4 is done.**
3. **Then system audio** in the live program: `--system`, loopback, and solving D-010 (no loopback data during silence). For first tests we can use a YouTube video with headphones. The headset-mic issue doesn't matter for system-only tests.

## System audio: plan (budget about 1.5 h, so roughly 18:45)

### Two problems to solve, both found by our own tests

**1. Loopback sends no data during silence (D-010).** This breaks two things on the system side:
- **The end of a phrase might never be detected.** VAD waits for silence that never arrives.
- **The timestamps and latency calculation would drift.** They assume the audio arrives without gaps, which we verified for the mic but which is false for loopback.

**Proposed solution: a silent "keep-alive" stream.** The program itself plays **digital silence** (all zeros, completely inaudible) on your speakers. Windows then treats the speakers as active, and loopback keeps delivering blocks continuously, silence included. Both problems disappear together. This is a commonly suggested workaround, but **I haven't verified it here**, so we test it first. The fallback, if it doesn't work, is a clock-based "no data for 0.5 s means the phrase ended", plus inserting silence for the gaps. That's more complex, so it's only worth doing if needed.

**2. One VAD model can't be shared by two streams.** I checked: Silero's model **keeps internal state** between windows; it remembers the recent audio. If the mic and system streams used the same model, their states would mix. So each stream gets **its own VAD model**. It's small, so that's cheap.

### Steps

**Step 1: verify the keep-alive (about 15 min).**
- Add a `--keep-alive` flag to `record_test.py`, plus a small `SilentOutput` class in `audio_capture.py`. The class finds the speaker device that belongs to the loopback device (same name without "[Loopback]"), and **fails loudly** if it can't find it.
- Test: **nothing playing**, 10 s. Without the flag the system stream gets 0 blocks (known); **with** the flag, we expect about 10 s of blocks.
- Then a second run with a video, to check that the video is still captured normally and you still hear it.

**Step 2: both streams in the live program (about 45 min).**
- `--system N`, defaulting to the loopback of the default speakers and printed at start.
- One capture plus one segmentation thread **per stream**, and **one shared processing thread**. The GPU handles one phrase at a time, so a phrase may wait, and the `queue` number shows it.
- The **time label comes from one session clock** for both streams, so `[00:01:12]` means the same moment on both sides.
- System-side label: **"Speaker ?"** for now. Real Speaker 1 / 2 labels come in M5.
- The shutdown waits for **both** segmentation threads.

**Step 3: test (about 20 min).** An Armenian YouTube video in headphones while you also speak. We check that both labels appear, the latency stays under 5 s, nothing is lost, and the timing is correct.

**About headphones:** your current headphones force the weak headset mic. For these tests that's acceptable, because we're checking the **system side**. Just don't judge "Me" accuracy today.

## Step 2: both streams in the live program (needs your OK)

The design is unchanged from what I described before:

- **`--system N`**: the loopback device, defaulting to the loopback of the default speakers, printed at start. It refuses a non-loopback device. **`SilentOutput` starts automatically** together with the system capture.
- **Per stream:** its own capture, its own VAD model (Silero keeps internal state, so it can't be shared), and its own segmentation thread.
- **Shared:** one phrase queue and one processing thread (Whisper, then NLLB, then print), labelled **"Me"** for mic phrases and **"Speaker ?"** for system phrases until M5.
- **One session clock:** `[hh:mm:ss]` and the latency are computed from each stream's own start time, so both sides line up.
- **Shutdown:** the processing thread finishes only after **both** segmentation threads have sent STOP. The exit summary shows **detected / printed per stream**, so a lost phrase on either side is visible.

Loading takes a few seconds longer (a second VAD model). Everything else stays the same.

I've rewritten `hylive/__main__.py` for two streams, and the syntax checks out. I kept a copy of the mic-only version outside the project, and Git has it anyway in the last commit.

## What changed, compared with the mic-only version

| Part | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Devices | `--mic` | `--mic` **and `--system`** (defaults: the Windows mic, and the loopback of the default speakers). A non-loopback device passed as `--system` is refused with an error |
| Keep-alive | — | `SilentOutput` is found at start-up, printed, started just before capture and stopped at the end (D-010) |
| VAD | 1 model | **One model per source**, because the Silero model remembers recent audio internally |
| Threads | 1 segmentation + 1 processing | **2 segmentation** (one per source) plus **1 shared processing** thread |
| Labels | always "Me" | **"Me"** for the mic, **"Speaker ?"** for the system side (M5 makes that Speaker 1/2) |
| Time `[hh:mm:ss]` | position in the mic stream | **One session clock**, so both sides show the same time for the same moment |
| Shutdown | ends after 1 STOP | The processing thread **ends only after 2 STOPs**, so both streams' last phrases are printed |
| Exit summary | one line | **One line per source**: detected / printed / PortAudio problem flags |

Unchanged: the ASR and translation settings, the latency line (now per source), the Event-based waiting (D-017), and fail-loudly on thread errors.

## Tests (headphones on)

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m hylive
```

**Test 1: system audio only.** After "Ready", play an **Armenian YouTube video** (news or an interview) for about **30–45 s** and **stay silent yourself**. **Pause the video once for about 3 seconds** in the middle. This checks that the phrase before the pause still gets closed and printed, which is the keep-alive in real use. Then wait until the output stops, and press Ctrl+C.

**Expected:**
- the blocks are labelled **`Speaker ?`**, with plausible Armenian and English;
- the latency is under 5 s;
- the summary shows `system ... detected N ... printed N` and `mic ... detected 0`.

**Test 2: both sides.** Start again. Play the video, and **say a few short Armenian sentences in between**, at least once **while the video is talking**. Then wait, and press Ctrl+C.

**Expected:**
- both **`Me`** and **`Speaker ?`** blocks appear, in time order;
- when two phrases end close together, one shows **`queue 1`**, and its latency is higher. Please note how high: this is the GPU-sharing risk we expected;
- for both sources, **detected = printed**.

Your "Me" text will be poor in these tests, because of the headset mic. That's expected; just check that it appears.

Both streams work, but this test found the **most important problem so far: latency is over 5 s for long phrases**.

## What works ✅

- **Both sources run at the same time.** The labels are correct, and **Me** and **Speaker ?** blocks appear in time order.
- **The keep-alive does its job in real use:** phrases on the system side get closed and printed, including during pauses.
- **Nothing lost:** mic 1/1 and system 8/8 detected = printed (one of them rescued at shutdown). **0 problem flags.**
- The video's Armenian is partly recognised (some names, «ամբողջ թիմի որոշումն է եղել…»), and some translations carry the meaning. The quality is rough, as expected.

## The problem: latency ❌

| Block | Phrase | ASR | Translation | **Latency** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 00:00:01 | long, continuous speech | 5.3 s | 2.1 s | **7.5 s** |
| 00:00:12 | long | 4.2 s | 2.3 s | **6.6 s** |
| 00:00:22 | long | 3.5 s | 1.7 s | **5.8 s** |
| 00:00:36 | **short** | 2.2 s | 0.7 s | ✅ 3.1 s |
| 00:00:46 | long | 4.2 s | 2.4 s | **6.7 s** |
| 00:00:56 | long | 6.1 s | 2.1 s | **8.4 s** |
| 00:01:06 | medium | 2.9 s | 1.2 s | ✅ 4.3 s |
| 00:01:14 **Me** | short | 1.7 s | 0.6 s | ⚠️ 5.0 s (waited about 2.7 s in the queue behind a Speaker phrase) |
| 00:01:16 | medium | 3.4 s | 1.3 s | ⚠️ 4.9 s |

**The cause is clear:** a news presenter speaks almost without pauses, so phrases grow to our **10-second maximum**. Both **ASR time and translation time grow with the number of words**. Your own read sentences were short, which is why we didn't see this before. Long phrases also make the **queue** problem worse: your short "Me" phrase had to wait for a long Speaker phrase.

## Proposed fix: shorter maximum phrase length (no code change; the flag exists)

| Run | Command |
|---|---|
| A | `.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m hylive --max-segment-s 5` |
| B (if A isn't enough) | `.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m hylive --max-segment-s 4` |

- **Same test as before:** the same video (ideally the same part), about 45 s, staying silent.
- **Decision rule, set now:** choose the **largest** maximum length for which **every** block is **≤ 5 s**. Longer phrases give the translator more context, so we don't go shorter than needed.
- **Expected trade-off:** sentences get cut in the middle more often, which makes some translations choppier. That's acceptable for the 5-second rule; we'll see how bad it is.
- If even 4 s isn't enough, the next lever is translation time (2+ s on the CPU for long text), for example by trying NLLB on the GPU. That would be measured separately.

## One question

**The "Me" block «Միմի այդ չէ իրական»: was that you speaking?** The next Speaker block contains very similar words («Միմիան, չէ, իրականում…»). If you **didn't** say it, then the headset mic picked up **the video from your headphones**, a kind of echo. That would be one more reason for mic-less headphones in M5.

## What went wrong: one bad phrase blocked everything

**1. Whisper "repetition loops"** (D-009 again). The "Me" blocks show «Հայք եմ այդ այդ այդ այդ…»: Whisper got stuck repeating a word until it hit its maximum output length. That took **7–8 s of ASR**, and then NLLB spent **17–20 s** translating hundreds of repeated words ("for this for this for this…").

**2. A queue cascade.** While those garbage phrases were processed, new phrases kept arriving: `queue` climbed to **27**, and latency grew to **90 s**. One shared processing thread can't recover from that.

**3. Echo is the likely trigger.** There are many more "Me" blocks than you probably spoke. As in Test 1, the headset mic picks up the video from your headphones. That quiet, echoed audio is exactly the kind of input that makes Whisper loop, and it **doubles the workload**. What did you actually say? That helps me tell your phrases from the echo.

(The `KeyboardInterrupt` traceback at the end is just the second Ctrl+C forcing an exit while it was still working through the queue. That's expected.)

## Proposed fixes: bound the time each phrase can take

I checked that the installed faster-whisper supports every option below (`max_new_tokens`, and `compression_ratio` on each result).

| # | Change | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **F1** | **Cap Whisper's output at 128 tokens** (`max_new_tokens`). If the cap is hit, the block is **marked visibly** "(cut at token limit)" | A loop can no longer take 7–8 s. 5 s of normal Armenian needs well under 128 tokens |
| **F2** | **Repetition guard:** Whisper reports a *compression ratio* for its output (repetitive text compresses extremely well). Above **2.4** (Whisper's own standard threshold), the block is printed as **"HY: (repetitive output discarded: likely noise or echo)"**, and **no translation** is done | No 20-second translations of garbage. It's **visible, not silent** |
| **F3** | **Cap the translation length** at about 2× the input length (`max_decoding_length`) | Translation time stays proportional to the input |
| **F4** | **The default maximum phrase length becomes 5 s** (it was 10) | Fixes the Test 1 latency (5.8–8.4 s) |
| **F5** | **`--sources mic,system`** (default: both), a **testing aid** to run one side alone | Until the headphones are fixed, we can test the system side **without echo**. It changes nothing in normal use |

**Not changing:** the decoding itself (temperature 0, beam 1). Options like `no_repeat_ngram_size` would change the accuracy, so they'd need a new eval run. They're a later option, only if F1 and F2 aren't enough.

## Tests after the fix

1. **`--sources system`**, the video only. Check that **every block is ≤ 5 s**, `queue` stays at 0–1, and detected = printed.
2. **Both sources**, with you speaking. Check that the latency stays bounded even with echo, and whether garbage now shows as "discarded" instead of blocking the queue.
3. A **quick rerun of `eval_asr.py`**, to make sure F1 didn't cut any of your 10 sentences (the CER should stay at 8.6%).

**Time:** 17:55. The system-audio block is at about 50 minutes of its 1.5 h. This fix is really **M6 (latency and reliability) pulled forward**, since it's now the critical problem. Total about 8.2 h.

May I make changes F1–F5?

All five fixes are in, and every file passes the syntax check. The system-audio block started at 17:07; it's now about 17:57.

## What changed

**`hylive/asr.py` (F1, plus the data for F2)**
- `MAX_NEW_TOKENS = 128` is passed to Whisper as `max_new_tokens`, so a repetition loop now stops at 128 tokens.
- A new **`transcribe_full()`** returns an `AsrResult`: the **text**, its **compression ratio**, and whether the **token limit was hit**. Its `.repetitive` property is true when the ratio is above **2.4**.
- `transcribe()` still returns only the text, so the eval scripts keep working. They go through the same limited decoding, so the eval rerun checks F1 too.

**`hylive/translate.py` (F3)**
- `max_decoding_length = 2 × input tokens + 10`, so translation time stays proportional to the input.

**`hylive/__main__.py` (F2, F4, F5)**
- **F2:** if Whisper's output is repetitive, the block shows **"HY: (repetitive output discarded - likely noise or echo; compression ratio X)"**, with no translation. If the token limit was hit, **"(cut at token limit)"** is added to the text. The exit summary now also counts **discarded** phrases per source.
- **F4:** the default `--max-segment-s` is now **5.0**.
- **F5:** `--sources mic`, `system` or `mic,system` (the default). In single-source mode it prints **"NOTE: testing mode"**, and the keep-alive only starts when the system side is captured. Invalid values are refused with an error.

The three tests show that the fixes worked for **single-side** use and found the next limit for **two-sided** use.

## Test 1: eval rerun ✅

**CER 8.6%, identical to before.** The 128-token cap didn't cut any of your sentences.

## Test 2: system only (video, no echo) ✅ mostly

| | Before the fixes | **After** |
|---|---|---|
| Latency | 5.8–8.4 s on most blocks | **3.3–5.4 s**; 11 of 13 blocks ≤ 5 s |
| Worst | 8.4 s | 5.4 s (two blocks: once translation 2.2 s, once ASR 3.2 s plus waiting) |
| Lost / discarded | — | 13/13 printed, 0 discarded |

So the 5-second cut fixed the long-phrase problem. **85% of blocks are under 5 s.** Our target in `TESTS.md` is 95%, so we're close but not there yet.

A small cosmetic issue: some lines end with **"�"** (e.g. «Առիս կ�»). When a phrase is cut at 5 s in the middle of a word, Whisper's last token can be **half an Armenian character**. It's harmless; I'll note it for later.

## Test 3: both sides ❌ throughput

| | |
|---|---|
| Phrases in about 50 s | **mic 13 + system 11 = 24** |
| Processing per phrase | about 2–3.5 s (ASR + translation, one after the other) |
| Result | about 60 s of work for 50 s of audio, so the **queue grows to 9** and latency to **22 s** |

The fixes did their job: **no single phrase took more than about 3.5 s**, and the loop was **discarded** instead of taking 20 s. But **one GPU, processing one phrase at a time, can't keep up with two streams that are talking continuously.**

**This test is a worst case.** The echo makes the mic stream carry the video *as well as* your voice, so it's effectively two continuous streams. In a real call with mic-less headphones, your mic only produces phrases when you speak. Still, it shows that **we have no capacity margin**.

Your own sentences came through **surprisingly well**, for example «ընթացքում կմիացնեմ տեսանյութը և կխոսեմ միաժամանակ» → "I'm going to put the video together and talk at the same time."

## Proposal: two ways to process more phrases per second

**Step 1: measure `large-v3-turbo` (no code change, about 10 min, about 1.6 GB download).**
- The turbo model is large-v3 with a much smaller text-generating part (the decoder): **4 layers instead of 32**. Writing out the text is a big part of our ASR time, so it could be roughly **2× faster**. **For Armenian it may be less accurate**, and only measurement will tell.
- It's in faster-whisper's model list (`large-v3-turbo`), which I checked in the installed code.

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\eval_asr.py --model large-v3-turbo
```

- **Rule, set now:** adopt turbo if its **CER is ≤ 10.6%** (at most 2 points worse than 8.6%) **and** its ASR time is clearly lower. Otherwise keep large-v3.

**Step 2: translation in its own thread (a code change, about 20 min).**
- Right now the GPU waits while the CPU translates. With a separate translation thread, the GPU can **already transcribe the next phrase while the previous one is being translated**. Per phrase, throughput goes from *ASR + translation* to roughly *the slower of the two*, about 30% more phrases per second. **The latency of each single phrase doesn't change**; the waiting time in the queue shrinks.

**Then repeat tests 2 and 3**, measuring the share of blocks ≤ 5 s.

**The long-term fix for test 3 is still the hardware:** mic-less headphones or a TRRS→TRS adapter. It removes the echo and therefore half of the load.

**Time:** 18:10. The system-audio block is at about 1 h; the total is about 8.5 h. This throughput work is about 45 min, which still leaves enough for M5 (3.5 h), the README and the rehearsal.

Shall I go ahead with **step 1** (you run the turbo measurement)?

## Turbo result: rejected by our rule ❌

| | large-v3 (current) | large-v3-turbo |
|---|---|---|
| **CER** | **8.6%** | **23.0%** (the limit was 10.6%) |
| ASR avg / max | 1.70 s / 1.93 s | **0.93 s / 0.98 s** (about 1.8× faster) |

Turbo is as fast as hoped, but **far less accurate in Armenian**. Sentence 02 even came out in **Latin and Cyrillic letters** («Ljavëm, шнура…»), although we tell Whisper `language="hy"`. That fits what I'd expect from turbo's much smaller decoder: it has less capacity left for low-resource languages. **We keep large-v3.** This goes into the README as "considered, measured, rejected".

## Step 2: translation in its own thread (needs your OK)

**The idea:** today, a single processing thread does Whisper (GPU) **and then** NLLB (CPU) for each phrase, so the GPU sits idle during every translation. I'd split it into **two threads, connected by a queue**:

```
phrase queue → ASR thread (GPU: Whisper) → text queue → translation thread (CPU: NLLB + print)
```

- While phrase 1 is being **translated** on the CPU, phrase 2 is already being **transcribed** on the GPU.
- **Throughput:** about *max(ASR, translation)* per phrase instead of *ASR + translation*. With roughly 2.2 s + 0.9 s, that's about 30% more phrases per second.
- **One printer:** only the translation thread prints, so the order of the blocks stays the same.
- **Latency per phrase stays the same.** Only the time spent waiting in the queue shrinks.
- **Shutdown:** the ASR thread passes STOP on to the translation thread only after **all** sources have stopped. "Done" is set by the translation thread, so the counters still prove that nothing is lost.
- **The latency line** shows both queues: `queue 1+0` means 1 phrase waiting for ASR and 0 waiting for translation.

**Then repeat the two live tests:**
1. `--sources system` (video only). **Goal: ≥ 95% of blocks ≤ 5 s.**
2. Both sources (video plus your speech). Does the queue still grow, and how far?

**Time:** 18:12. The system-audio and latency block is at about 1 h 5 min; the total is about 8.6 h. May I make the change?

## What I've built

**1. Translation in its own thread** (`hylive/__main__.py`, syntax-checked):
- The old `process_phrases` is replaced by **`transcribe_phrases`** (GPU thread) and **`translate_and_print`** (CPU thread, the only one that prints), connected by a text queue.
- The STOP signal passes through the ASR thread to the translation thread only after **all** sources are done, and the "done" event is set by the translation thread.
- The latency line now shows `queue A+B`: **A** = phrases waiting for ASR, **B** = waiting for translation.
- **New in the exit summary, per source:** median latency, maximum latency, and the **share of blocks ≤ 5 s**, so you don't have to count by hand.

**2. `scripts/play_eval.py`, for a known transcript on the system side.** A YouTube video has no exact transcript, so CER would be impossible to compute. This script plays **your evaluation recordings through the speakers**. The live program hears them via loopback, as the "call side", and we know every word. It prints which sentence it plays, and when.

## Test protocol

You need **two PowerShell windows**, both started with `cd D:\Em\mathrix`, and headphones on.

### Test A: system audio only (about 45 s, 6 clips, known text 01–06)

- **Window 1:** `.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m hylive --sources system`
- Wait for **"Ready"**, then in **Window 2:**

  ```powershell
  .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\play_eval.py --ids 01,02,03,04,05,06
  ```

- Stay silent. When Window 2 prints `done`, wait about 5 s, then press **Ctrl+C** in Window 1.

### Test B: both streams (about 60 s)

- **System side:** clips 01–05, 7 s apart.
- **Mic side:** **you read sentences 06–10 aloud**, one in each pause.

- **Window 1:** `.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m hylive`
- Wait for **"Ready"**, then in **Window 2:**

  ```powershell
  .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\play_eval.py --ids 01,02,03,04,05 --gap 7 --start-delay 6
  ```

- **Read 06** during the first 6 s (before clip 01 starts). Then read **07, 08, 09, 10**, one in each 7-second pause after a clip:
  - 06 Կարո՞ղ ես կրկնել վերջին նախադասությունը։
  - 07 Երեկ երեկոյան անձրև էր գալիս։
  - 08 Բժիշկը վաղը առավոտյան կզանգահարի։
  - 09 Մեր հանդիպումը տեղափոխվել է հաջորդ շաբաթ։
  - 10 Ես սիրում եմ սուրճ խմել աշխատանքից առաջ։
- After `done`, wait about 5 s, then press Ctrl+C.

**Paste both windows' output for each test.** I'll then compute, **separately for mic and system**:
- **CER** against the known text, compared with the file-based eval (8.6% over 10 sentences);
- the **English** judged per sentence (correct / gist / wrong), compared with M4;
- **latency** (median, max, % ≤ 5 s), **queue sizes**, **discarded** count, and **detected vs printed**, compared with the earlier runs;
- for Test B, **how many "Me" blocks are echo** of the played clips rather than your voice.

**Two things to expect:**
- Your mic phrases go through the **headset mic**, so their CER will be worse than in the eval set. That measures the current hardware, honestly.
- The headset mic will probably also pick up the played clips: that's the echo, and we'll count it.

**Time:** 18:16. The system-audio and latency block is at about 1 h 10 min; the total is about 8.7 h. The two tests plus analysis take about 20 min.

## 2. Separation of "Me" and the call: echo confirmed

**About 5 of the 11 "Me" blocks are echo of the video**, not your voice. They appear 2–3 s after the matching Speaker block, with almost the same words:

| Speaker ? | → "Me" (echo) |
|---|---|

So about a quarter of all phrases in this run were **duplicate work caused by echo**, and they're wrongly labelled "Me".

## 3. Latency and queues, compared with the earlier runs

| | Both streams, before | **Now (translation thread)** |
|---|---|---|
| Max queue | **9** (still growing) | **4+0**, and it went back to 0 |
| Max latency | 22 s | **8.7 s** |
| Mic ≤ 5 s | — | 7/11 (**64%**), median 4.8 s |

**The translation thread worked:** the translation queue (the second number) was **0 almost always**, and the system recovered instead of piling up. **The bottleneck is now only ASR on the GPU**, at about 1.5–3 s per phrase.

**The pattern over time is the key finding:**
- **0–20 s** (video + echo + you): queue up to 4, latency **5–8.7 s** ❌
- **From 24 s**: queue 0–1, latency **2.4–4.3 s** ✅

**Conclusion:** with **one side talking at a time**, it's comfortably under 5 s. **With overlap plus echo**, about 0.45 phrases per second × about 2 s each fills the GPU about 90% of the time, and peaks go over 5 s.

## My recommendation

1. **The biggest, cheapest fix is the hardware.** Mic-less headphones or a TRRS→TRS adapter removes the echo, which is **about a quarter of the load** and **all of the wrongly labelled "Me" blocks**. It's now clearly the most important open item for the interview.

| | Both streams, before | **Now (translation thread)** |
|---|---|---|

**The translation thread worked:** the translation queue (the second number) was **0 almost always**, and the system recovered instead of piling up. **The bottleneck is now only ASR on the GPU**, at about 1.5–3 s per phrase.

**The pattern over time is the key finding:**
- **0–20 s** (video + echo + you): queue up to 4, latency **5–8.7 s** ❌
- **From 24 s**: queue 0–1, latency **2.4–4.3 s** ✅

**Conclusion:** with **one side talking at a time**, it's comfortably under 5 s. **With overlap plus echo**, about 0.45 phrases per second × about 2 s each fills the GPU about 90% of the time, and peaks go over 5 s.

Right, today the aim is **M5 first, fast and focused**. The repo is clean (last commit `1997bc5`), and today's block started at **17:40**. The new target is **Oct 30**, with about 10.8 h of budget left.

## M5 plan (budget about 3 h)

**How speaker identification works, simply:**
1. For every call-side phrase, a small neural network computes a **"voice fingerprint"**, called an *embedding*: a list of 192 numbers describing *how* the voice sounds, not *what* is said.
2. **Online clustering:** the new fingerprint is compared with each known speaker's average fingerprint, using **cosine similarity** (1 = identical, 0 = unrelated).
   - If it's **above a threshold**, it's the same person, so the label is reused and that speaker's average is updated.
   - Otherwise it's a **new speaker**, `Speaker N+1`.
3. **Very short phrases** (under about 1 s) give unreliable fingerprints. How to label them is a decision we'll make from the data.

**Model:** SpeechBrain **ECAPA-TDNN** (`speechbrain/spkrec-ecapa-voxceleb`), a widely used speaker-verification model that runs on the CPU. **What I could not verify online today** (the PyPI pages were blocked) is its exact dependencies with our torch 2.14. In particular, SpeechBrain has historically required `torchaudio`. So the first step checks this **without installing anything**.

## Step 1 (in parallel, about 5 min)

**1a. Dependency check.** This is a dry run that only *shows* what would be installed:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --dry-run speechbrain
```

Paste the last lines, especially `Would install ...`. If it wants to replace our `torch 2.14.1+cpu` or pulls in something large or strange, we stop and choose an alternative before anything is changed.

**1b. Record test material: 2 voices, about 60 s.** Find an Armenian **interview with two speakers who alternate** (ideally a man and a woman for the first test; later two similar voices). Play it in headphones and run:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\record_test.py --seconds 60 --keep-alive --label twovoices
```

We'll only use the `_system.wav` file. It's ignored by Git, like all recordings.

## The steps after that (each one short)

2. Install SpeechBrain if the dry run looks safe, and pin it in `requirements.txt`.
3. **`scripts/speaker_test.py`** (offline): cuts the recording into phrases with our segmenter, saves them as numbered WAVs, computes a fingerprint for each, and prints the labels for **several thresholds** side by side, plus the embedding time per phrase.
4. **Ground truth:** you listen to the phrase files and mark each one as A or B. We then **count label errors per threshold** and pick the best by numbers.
5. **`hylive/speakers.py`**, built into the live program: the fingerprint is computed in the translation thread (CPU), so the GPU isn't slowed down. Then a live test with `--sources system`.

Run 1a and 1b, and paste both outputs.

That's the right question to ask. The brief says *"Keep it basic"* and allows *"any libraries and models you like, as long as they run locally"*. Mathrix's tips warn against unnecessary complexity. Speaker identification itself **is mandatory**, so the real question is **which option is simplest *overall* while still working reliably**.

## Options, judged on simplicity *and* reliability

| Option | New dependencies | Our own code | Reliability for telling voices apart | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A: plain audio statistics** (e.g. average pitch or MFCCs with numpy) | none | small | **Poor.** Two men or two women with similar voices get mixed up; easily thrown off by noise and call compression | ❌ looks simple, but would fail the live test |
| **B: reuse Whisper's internal "encoder" output** as a fingerprint | none | medium | **Unproven.** Whisper is trained to *ignore* who speaks. It would also add GPU work, and the GPU is already our bottleneck | ❌ |
| **C: an ONNX speaker model** through `onnxruntime` (already installed) | none via pip, but a model file to find and verify | **More**: we'd have to reimplement the model's exact audio preprocessing (filterbank features) ourselves; a small mismatch silently ruins accuracy | Good, *if* done exactly right | ⚠️ fewer packages, but more custom code and more risk |
| **D: SpeechBrain ECAPA** (a standard pretrained speaker model) | **1 package**, plus its small helpers | **Minimal**: load the model, then one call per phrase. Preprocessing is built in | Good and widely used for exactly this task; runs on the CPU with the torch we **already have** for VAD | ✅ *if* its dependencies are light |

**My view:** **D** is the simplest *solution*: the least code to write, read and explain in the interview, and a proven model. C saves one package but adds hand-written signal processing, which is exactly the kind of hidden complexity the tips warn about. **A and B are simpler only on paper.**

**The one unknown is D's dependency cost.** I couldn't verify it online, because the PyPI pages were blocked today.

## Proposed decision rule (set before we look)

Run the **dry run**. It installs **nothing**:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --dry-run speechbrain
```

- **Accept D** if it only adds **small helper packages** and **does not replace or upgrade `torch`** (2.14.1+cpu, which must stay).
- **Reject D and switch to C** if it wants to **change torch**, or pulls in **large packages** (hundreds of MB), or anything unexpected. I'd then verify a specific ONNX speaker model and its exact preprocessing before writing any code.

Paste the dry-run output, especially the `Would install …` line, and we decide in one step. Recording the 2-voice material (step 1b) is useful for **either** option, so you can do that in parallel.

## Checking it against our rule

| Criterion | Result |
|---|---|
| Replaces or upgrades `torch`? | ✅ **No.** `torch 2.14.1` "already satisfied" and stays |
| Large packages? | ✅ None of hundreds of MB. The largest is **scipy** (tens of MB); the rest are small helpers (YAML, requests, soundfile, sentencepiece) |
| Anything unexpected? | ⚠️ **One risk:** `torchaudio-2.11.0` would be installed next to our **torch 2.14.1**. torchaudio is normally built for *one exact* torch version. pip allows the combination, but it may fail when imported |

**By the rule, D is accepted, with one condition:** right after installing, we run a **short smoke test**. If `speechbrain` or `torchaudio` fails to load, or the model doesn't work, we **uninstall these exact packages** (the list above) and switch to option C. Undoing it would be quick and clean.

## What I created

**`hylive/speakers.py`**, about 60 lines:
- **`SpeakerEncoder`** loads ECAPA once, on the CPU, downloading it into `models\` (about 80 MB, once). Its `embed(audio)` returns a fingerprint normalised to length 1, which makes cosine similarity simply a dot product.
- **`SpeakerTracker(threshold)`**, the online clustering. `assign(fingerprint)` compares the fingerprint with each known speaker's *average* fingerprint, which is updated as more phrases arrive. It returns the label **and the best similarity**, so we can always see *why* a label was chosen.

**`scripts/speaker_test.py <wav>`**, the offline test:
- It cuts phrases **exactly like the live program** (VAD, maximum 5 s).
- It saves them as `recordings\segments\<name>\segNN.wav`, so you can listen.
- It prints, **per phrase**, the label for **4 thresholds** (0.3 / 0.4 / 0.5 / 0.6), with the similarity score, the number of speakers found per threshold, and the **fingerprint time** (the latency cost).

## Steps

**1. Pin the new packages:**

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip freeze | Set-Content -Encoding ascii requirements.txt
```

**2. Record the 2-voice material** (an Armenian interview with two people alternating, headphones on, about 60 s):

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\record_test.py --seconds 60 --keep-alive --label twovoices
```

**3. Run the test** on the `_system.wav` file that step 2 prints:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\speaker_test.py recordings\<printed name>_twovoices_system.wav
```

**4. Ground truth:** play `seg01.wav`, `seg02.wav` and so on from the printed folder, and write **who speaks** in each, for example `01 A, 02 A, 03 B, 04 A/B (both)…`. That takes about 5 minutes for about 15 phrases.

Then I'll count the label errors per threshold and we choose by numbers.

**Possible issue on the first run:** the model download. If it fails, especially with a "symlink" or "privilege" error, paste it as it is.

**Time:** 18:06. M5 has used about 25 minutes; the total is about 9.6 h.

3. **Loopback is a digital copy of what Windows sends to your headphones.** It doesn't pass through any microphone, so your headset mic can't get into it. The echo we saw before goes the *other* way: the **mic** picking up the headphones. That only affects the `_mic` file, which this test didn't use.

**The one exception, for completeness:** if a Windows setting like **"Listen to this device"** were enabled for your microphone, Windows would play your mic through the headphones, and then it *would* appear in loopback. That's off by default, and our earlier tests showed no sign of it. You'll also hear it immediately when you listen to the segments: **if you hear only the two interview voices, and never yourself, the labels come purely from the interview.**

I've gone through the run. Short version: **the second speaker most likely *was* heard, around 01:01, but it was merged into Speaker 1.** Your own two sentences weren't involved at all.

## Did your own speech affect the test? No

You ran with **`--sources system`**, so the microphone wasn't recorded at all. Your two sentences never reached the program. That's correct for this test, and nothing to fix.

## Why only 1 speaker was found

Look at the **similarity** values. Each one shows how close a phrase was to the closest known voice:

| Time | Similarity | What it suggests |
|---|---|---|
| Most phrases | **0.70–0.85** | clearly the same voice (the man talking about «պորտալար») |
| 00:00:07 | 0.48 | the second phrase, compared with only **one** earlier phrase, so the average voice isn't stable yet |
| 00:00:50 «Հիտ!» | 0.12 | very short (< 1 s), so the short-phrase rule kept the existing label (by design) |
| **00:01:01** «**Միտես իմ հարցը** ավելի շտ որ կոնտեքստում է» ("…my question…") | **0.44** | **this sounds like the interviewer asking a question.** 0.44 is above the threshold of 0.35, so it was labelled Speaker 1 |

So the likely cause is that **in this video, the interviewer was heard only briefly, and their voice was more similar to the man's (0.44)** than in the offline recordings (0.14 / 0.21). Also, this doesn't look like the same part of the interview as the offline test: the offline recording changed speaker at about 14 s, and this run didn't.

**Latency is good:** median **3.9 s**, **93% ≤ 5 s**, maximum 5.3 s, with the speaker step taking only about 0.5 s. So speaker ID **didn't break the latency budget**.

## Two quick questions

1. **Who speaks at 01:01** («Միտես իմ հարցը…»): the interviewer, or the same man?
2. Was this **the same video, from the start**, as the offline same-gender recording, or a different one? And roughly **when did the second person speak**?

## A simple fix, if 01:01 is the interviewer

**Raise the default threshold from 0.35 to 0.45**, a one-number change. That fits **all** our data:

| | Values seen | At 0.45 |
|---|---|---|
| Same person (offline, ≥ 1 s) | ≥ **0.54** | stays the same speaker ✅ |
| Different person (offline) | **0.14, 0.21** | new speaker ✅ |
| Different person (live, 01:01) | **0.44** | new speaker ✅ |
| Mixed phrase at a speaker change (offline) | 0.46 | stays the earlier speaker ✅ |

**The risk** is the 00:00:07 phrase (**0.48**). If the same man is that close to 0.45 early on, the margin is thin. Before changing the default, I'd quickly **re-run the two offline recordings with `--thresholds 0.4,0.45,0.5`**, to confirm there are still 0 errors.

If **01:01 is the same man**, a threshold change would make things *worse*. Then the honest result is "this pair of voices is too similar for the model at this phrase length", documented as a limitation.

Both are good questions. Here's what the data says about each, with a quick test plan that doesn't add complexity.

## 1. Do we still need the headphone adapter?

**Maybe not, but one clean run doesn't prove it.** The echo appeared in **3 earlier runs** (on Oct 25 about 5 of 11 "Me" blocks were echo), and **not in L2**. The difference was probably the **video volume**. In the interview, the call volume and the number of people talking aren't under our control.

**A simple, data-driven check (about 3 min):**
- Play an interview **at the volume you'd use in the real interview**.
- **Stay completely silent** for about 60 s, with the full program running (`python -m hylive`).
- **Count the "Me" blocks.** They should be **0**.

If it's 0, **we keep the current setup**, and the README notes "keep call volume moderate; echo handling is out of scope". If "Me" blocks appear, the adapter is worth buying. We'd decide by evidence, not by guessing.

## 2. Natural and mixed Armenian

**What the brief says:** *"languages other than Armenian as input"* is **out of scope**. So we don't need to *support* Russian or English input. But everyday Armenian **with borrowed words** («короче», «давай», "meeting", "deadline") **is** realistic Armenian speech, and the interviewers will speak naturally. It's worth knowing what happens.

**What I expect, but haven't tested:**
- We force Whisper to `language="hy"`, so Russian and English words will probably be **written in Armenian letters** («կարոչե», «միթինգ»), or mangled.
- NLLB may then not recognise them, or may guess wrongly.
- Colloquial forms («ոնց ես», «կարում», «էսօր») may be recognised better than the formal sentences, because Whisper learned from real speech. That's unknown.

**About Բ→Վ:** we already tried the cheap knobs (beam 5, a prompt, padding), and none fixed it. I don't see a *general* simple fix that doesn't cost latency. The only zero-latency option would be a **small correction list** (e.g. «Վարև» → «Բարև»). That's quick, but it's a patch for specific words, not a real fix, and it could hide errors. I'd only consider it if the test shows a few **very frequent** words failing consistently, and I'd document it openly.

### Test plan (about 25 min, no new models)

**A small code change:** a `--set` option for `record_eval.py`, `eval_asr.py` and `play_eval.py`, so a second sentence list (`eval/sentences_mixed.txt`, audio in `eval/audio/mixed/`) can be used. The existing evaluation set stays unchanged.

| Colloquial | Հալա ուրեմն վաղը կտեսնեմ ենք | So I'll see you tomorrow. | ✅ |
| Russian «Давай» | **դամ** ազատլինը զանգի | The lady of liberty is calling. | ❌ the Russian word got mangled and broke the sentence |
| Russian «Ладно» | **լաֆ** հետոք խոսենք | Let's talk about it. | ⚠️ gist |
| English "meeting", "deadline" | **միթինգը** … **դիլնայնը** … երկու շապյա | Our meeting has been moved, and the Dillane is now a two-piece. | ⚠️ "meeting" ✅; "deadline" ❌; «երկուշաբթի» (Monday) ❌ |
| English "ok", "link", "chat" | **Ոգեյ**, ես կեզ **լինքը** գողարկեմ **չատով** | Okay, I'm going to steal the cat. | ❌ «ուղարկեմ» became «գողարկեմ» ("steal"), and «չատով» ("chat") became "cat" |

**Latency: 7/7 ≤ 5 s** (median 3.2 s), and one noise fragment was correctly **discarded**.

## Conclusions

1. **Colloquial Armenian without foreign words works about as well as formal Armenian.** The informal forms («ոնց ես», «ուրեմն») came through fine.
2. **Foreign words are written in Armenian letters** (միթինգ, դիլնայն, լինք, չատ), because we force `language="hy"`. Translation sometimes recovers them ("meeting", "Okay") and sometimes doesn't ("Dillane", "cat").
3. **Russian discourse words** (Давай, Ладно) are mangled, and can derail a whole sentence.
4. **There's no simple, latency-free fix**, and mixed-language input is out of scope in the brief. **Decision: document it as a known limitation** with these examples, and move on. I'll add this to `TESTS.md` with the next docs update.

The offline check found a real problem, which is exactly why we ran it.

## What happened

| Step | Offline? |
|---|---|
| VAD (Silero) | ✅ loaded |
| Whisper large-v3 | ✅ loaded |
| **NLLB tokenizer** (`transformers`) | ❌ it **tried to contact huggingface.co** to check for file updates, retried for about 30 s, and would have failed |

**The models themselves are all local.** The NLLB *tokenizer* (the part that splits text into word pieces) **checks online for newer files** by default. Without internet, it retries and fails. The brief says all processing must run locally, and in the interview a missing Wi-Fi connection would break the start-up. The `torch.jit` warning is gone, as intended.

## Fix: strict offline mode, plus a one-time download script

1. **`hylive/__main__.py`:** at the very top, before any library is imported, set **`HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`**. That's the official Hugging Face switch meaning "use only local files, never contact the server". It applies to all libraries that use Hugging Face: Whisper, the NLLB tokenizer and SpeechBrain. The start-up message says so openly.
2. **A new `scripts/download_models.py`:** a one-time setup step, **run with internet**, that downloads Whisper, the NLLB tokenizer and the speaker model into `models\`. The README then says: install → download models → convert NLLB → run (offline).

I'm making this change now.

## What happened

| Step | Offline? |
|---|---|
| VAD (Silero) | ✅ loaded |
| Whisper large-v3 | ✅ loaded |
| **NLLB tokenizer** (`transformers`) | ❌ it **tried to contact huggingface.co** to check for file updates, retried for about 30 s, and would have failed |

**The models themselves are all local.** The NLLB *tokenizer* (the part that splits text into word pieces) **checks online for newer files** by default. Without internet, it retries and fails. The brief says all processing must run locally, and in the interview a missing Wi-Fi connection would break the start-up. The `torch.jit` warning is gone, as intended.

## Fix: strict offline mode, plus a one-time download script

1. **`hylive/__main__.py`:** at the very top, before any library is imported, set **`HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`**. That's the official Hugging Face switch meaning "use only local files, never contact the server". It applies to all libraries that use Hugging Face: Whisper, the NLLB tokenizer and SpeechBrain. The start-up message says so openly.
2. **A new `scripts/download_models.py`:** a one-time setup step, **run with internet**, that downloads Whisper, the NLLB tokenizer and the speaker model into `models\`. The README then says: install → download models → convert NLLB → run (offline).

Character error rate (CER) was 8.6 % on\n  clearly read sentences, but small spelling errors often change the meaning of the English translation.\n\n---\n\n## Contents\n1. Check that the GPU works (downloads Whisper \"tiny\", ~75 MB)\n.\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe scripts\\gpu_smoke_test.py          # must end with \"SUCCESS\"\n\n# 3. Download the models into models\\ (needs internet, once: Whisper large-v3 ~3 GB, NLLB tokenizer, speaker model)\n.\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe scripts\\download_models.py\n\n# 4.
